topics.title: Document Structure
topics.summary: Learn the required skeleton of every HTML document and how the DOCTYPE controls browser rendering mode.

lessons.title: The HTML Skeleton
lessons.contentMarkdown:
Every HTML document starts from the same basic skeleton. Understanding this skeleton is the foundation for everything else you will learn, because every page you build - no matter how complex - sits on top of it. ## The Four Core Pieces A minimal HTML5 document contains four pieces, always in this order: - `` - tells the browser to render the page in standards mode using the HTML5 rules. - `` - the root element that wraps the entire document. - `` - contains metadata about the page: its title, character encoding, linked stylesheets, scripts, and so on. Nothing inside `` is displayed directly on the page. - `` - contains everything the user actually sees and interacts with: text, images, forms, buttons, and more. ```html My First Page

Hello, world!

This is my first HTML page.

``` ## Why the lang Attribute Matters Notice the `lang="en"` attribute on ``. It tells screen readers which pronunciation and hyphenation rules to use, and it helps browsers and translation tools identify the page's primary language. Always set it to match the language your content is written in. ## Nesting Rules HTML elements nest inside one another like boxes. `` and `` are both direct children of `` and must not overlap - every tag you open must be closed before its parent closes. Browsers are forgiving and will silently try to "fix" broken markup, but relying on that is risky, since different browsers repair different mistakes in different ways. Always close your tags properly. ## A Note on Case and Quotes Tag and attribute names are conventionally written in lowercase in modern HTML, and attribute values are wrapped in double quotes. Neither is strictly enforced by the parser, but both are the convention used by every major style guide, and mixing styles makes code harder to read and maintain.

This is my first HTML page.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a blank white page with a large 'Hello, world!' heading followed by a paragraph of text; the browser tab shows the title 'My First Page'.

lessons.title: DOCTYPE and Browser Rendering Modes
lessons.contentMarkdown:
The very first line of an HTML document, ``, looks like a leftover from old SGML-based HTML, but in HTML5 it has exactly one practical job: it switches the browser into **standards mode**. ## Standards Mode vs Quirks Mode Before HTML5 existed, browsers had to support pages written against very old, inconsistent rendering rules. To stay backward compatible, every modern browser still ships two or three rendering modes: - **Standards mode** - the browser follows the modern CSS and HTML specifications as closely as possible. - **Quirks mode** - the browser emulates non-standard behavior from 1990s browsers, including odd box-model sizing, loose table cell layout, and case-insensitive matching of certain values. - **Limited ("almost standards") mode** - a mostly-standards mode with a couple of quirks kept for backward compatibility, mainly around table cell sizing and image vertical alignment. A missing, misspelled, or incomplete DOCTYPE silently drops the page into quirks mode, which can cause confusing CSS layout bugs because the HTML and CSS look perfectly correct while the browser measures boxes differently. ```html Standards Mode Example

This page renders using modern CSS box-sizing rules because of the DOCTYPE above.

``` ## Why HTML5's DOCTYPE Is So Simple Older doctypes for HTML 4.01 or XHTML 1.0 were long and referenced external Document Type Definitions, for example: ``` ``` HTML5 dropped the DTD entirely; the spec no longer validates documents against that kind of formal grammar. The doctype was simplified to the shortest string that reliably triggers standards mode in every browser: ``. It is case-insensitive, but lowercase is the universal convention. ## Practical Takeaway Always put `` as the very first line of every HTML document, with nothing - not even whitespace or a comment - before it. Treat it as non-negotiable boilerplate, the same way you would always terminate a statement in a C-family language.

codeExamples.description: Correct placement of the DOCTYPE as the very first line, before any other markup or comments
codeExamples.code: Box sizes and layout follow modern CSS rules, not legacy quirks-mode behavior.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a paragraph of text; because <!DOCTYPE html> is the very first line of the file, the browser uses standards mode for all layout and CSS calculations instead of legacy quirks mode.

codeExamples.description: The old, verbose HTML 4.01 Strict doctype, shown for comparison with HTML5's simplified version
codeExamples.code: This still triggers standards mode in modern browsers, but is far more verbose than HTML5's doctype.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Also renders in standards mode in every modern browser, demonstrating that the long HTML 4.01 doctype and the one-line HTML5 doctype achieve the same practical rendering-mode result today, which is why virtually all new projects use the much shorter HTML5 form.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the purpose of `<!DOCTYPE html>`, and what happens if you omit it?
interviewQuestions.answer:
`` is a declaration placed on the very first line of an HTML document. Its job is to tell the browser which rendering rules to use when laying out and styling the page. In HTML5, the doctype is deliberately short because it no longer references any formal grammar file - it exists purely as a signal. When the browser sees a valid doctype as the first line, it renders the page in **standards mode**, following modern CSS and HTML specifications. If you omit the doctype, misspell it, or put anything before it, the browser falls back to **quirks mode**, which emulates inconsistent, non-standard behavior from older browsers (different box-model math, different handling of percentage heights, and more). This can cause layout bugs that are hard to diagnose because the markup and CSS look correct. ```html Example

Rendered in standards mode.

``` The practical rule: always include `` as the literal first line of every page.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A developer notices that padding and width calculations look different on an old internal tool page compared to every other page on the same site, even though the CSS files are identical.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Assuming the doctype only matters for HTML validators; forgetting to add it when copy-pasting a fragment into a brand-new file; accidentally placing a comment or blank line before it, which some older browsers treat as content preceding the doctype.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
What is quirks mode, concretely, in terms of CSS behavior?
How can you check which rendering mode a page loaded in using browser developer tools?

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the `<head>` and `<body>` elements, and what kinds of content belong in each?
interviewQuestions.answer:
`` and `` are both required direct children of ``, and together they contain everything in a document, but they serve opposite purposes. **``** holds metadata - information *about* the page that is not rendered as visible content in the page flow. Typical children include: - `` - the text shown in the browser tab and used as the default bookmark name. - `<meta>` - character encoding, viewport settings, descriptions, and other key/value metadata. - `<link>` - references to external resources, most commonly stylesheets and icons. - `<style>` - embedded CSS. - `<script>` - JavaScript, though scripts are also commonly placed at the end of `<body>` or loaded with `defer`/`async`. **`<body>`** holds everything the user actually sees and interacts with: headings, paragraphs, images, forms, buttons, and so on. Only one `<body>` is allowed per document. ```html <head> <meta charset="UTF-8"> <title>Pricing - Acme Co

Our Pricing

``` A useful mental model: if removing a tag would change what text or graphics appear on the rendered page, it belongs in ``; if it only configures or describes the page, it belongs in ``.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A junior developer accidentally places an `<h1>` inside `<head>` while refactoring a page, and the heading silently disappears from the rendered output in some browsers while others render it oddly above the rest of the content.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Putting visible markup inside `<head>`; omitting `<title>` entirely, which hurts both usability and SEO; loading large render-blocking `<script>` tags in `<head>` without `defer` or `async`, which delays first paint.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
Which elements inside `<head>` can affect page-load performance, and how?
Why is it often recommended to place `<script>` tags just before the closing `</body>` tag, or use `defer`?

interviewQuestions.question: Explain the difference between quirks mode, limited-quirks ("almost standards") mode, and standards mode, and how a browser decides which one to apply.
interviewQuestions.answer:
Browsers support up to three distinct rendering modes to stay backward compatible with pages written before CSS was standardized:

1. **Quirks mode** - triggered by a missing doctype, certain very old doctypes, or malformed doctypes. The browser emulates pre-standardization behavior: for example, in quirks mode, table cells and images without explicit sizing can collapse differently, percentage-based heights behave inconsistently, and the box model may calculate width/height including padding and border by default (closer to `box-sizing: border-box` behavior) rather than the standards-mode content-box default.

2. **Limited-quirks mode** (also called "almost standards" mode) - triggered by certain transitional doctypes (e.g., HTML 4.01 Transitional with a URL). It is almost fully standards-compliant except for a narrow quirk around the vertical sizing of table cells containing images, kept specifically for legacy compatibility.

3. **Standards mode** - triggered by a valid HTML5 doctype (`<!DOCTYPE html>`) or a strict HTML4/XHTML doctype. The browser follows the CSS and HTML specifications without legacy accommodations.

The decision happens during the browser's "doctype sniffing" step, before the rest of the document is parsed: the parser inspects the literal doctype string (and, for older doctypes, whether a system identifier URL is present) and assigns a mode that then governs CSS box-model math, form element sizing, and a handful of other legacy behaviors for the entire document - it cannot be changed partway through a page.

This matters today mainly when maintaining legacy applications, embedding old content via iframes (each document has its own mode), or debugging why a page inside a CMS-generated wrapper looks subtly different from a hand-written one.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A legacy intranet application originally built in the early 2000s is migrated into a modern CSS framework, and several components render with incorrect spacing even though no CSS rules were changed, because the migrated page lost its original doctype.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Assuming all browsers implement quirks mode identically (minor differences exist); confusing browser 'quirks mode' with Internet Explorer's old 'Compatibility View' feature, which is a different, IE-specific mechanism; believing quirks mode can be toggled per-element rather than being a whole-document setting.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How would you confirm which rendering mode a given page is using, using browser developer tools?
Why did the HTML5 specification keep quirks mode instead of simply deprecating old documents?

topics.title: Common Text Elements & Attributes
topics.summary: Explore the everyday elements used to mark up text, and the global attributes available on almost every HTML element.

lessons.title: Headings, Paragraphs, and Text Formatting
lessons.contentMarkdown:
Most of the text on a web page is marked up using a small set of elements you will use constantly: headings, paragraphs, and inline formatting elements. ## Headings: h1 through h6 HTML provides six levels of heading, `

` (most important) through `

` (least important). Headings are not just bigger, bolder text - they define the structural outline of your document, which screen readers and search engines rely on to understand how content is organized. ```html

Article Title

Section Heading

Subsection Heading

``` A well-formed page typically has exactly one `

` describing the page's main topic, with `

` through `

` nested underneath to reflect the outline, similar to a table of contents. ## Paragraphs and Line Breaks The `

` element represents a paragraph of text. Browsers automatically add spacing above and below each paragraph. To force a line break *within* a paragraph (such as in a mailing address), use the self-closing `
` element - sparingly, since using it to fake paragraph spacing is a common anti-pattern that should be handled with CSS margins instead. ```html

123 Main Street
Springfield, USA

``` ## Inline Text Formatting HTML includes several inline elements for emphasizing or marking up specific words: - `` - marks text as having strong importance (rendered bold by default). - `` - marks text as stressed/emphasized (rendered italic by default). - `` - represents side comments or fine print. - `` - highlights text relevant to the current context, like a search result match. - `` / `` - subscript and superscript, useful for chemical formulas or footnotes. ```html

This step is required before continuing, and is not optional.

Water is H2O.

``` Each of these has a semantic meaning that benefits assistive technology, which is more robust than relying on `` and ``, the purely visual bold/italic elements covered in more detail in the interview questions for this topic.

codeExamples.description: A short article using a heading hierarchy, paragraphs, and inline formatting
codeExamples.code:
Getting Started with HTML

HTML is the foundational language of the web. It is not a programming language; it is a markup language.

Why It Matters

Every browser, screen reader, and search engine parses HTML to understand your content.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a large 'Getting Started with HTML' heading, a paragraph with the words 'foundational language' in bold and 'not' in italics, a smaller 'Why It Matters' subheading, and a second paragraph below it.

lessons.title: Global Attributes: id, class, style, and data-*
lessons.contentMarkdown:
Global attributes are attributes that can be applied to virtually any HTML element, regardless of its tag. Learning the most common ones early will make every other topic in HTML easier to follow. ## id The `id` attribute gives an element a unique identifier within the page. No two elements on the same page should share the same `id`. It is used for CSS targeting, JavaScript lookups (`document.getElementById`), and as the target of in-page links (`#section-2`). ```html

Pricing

Jump to pricing ``` ## class The `class` attribute assigns one or more space-separated class names to an element, used mainly for styling with CSS and selecting groups of elements with JavaScript. Unlike `id`, many elements can share the same class. ```html

Disk space is nearly full.

``` ## style The `style` attribute lets you apply CSS declarations directly to a single element. It is convenient for quick prototyping, but is generally discouraged in production code because it mixes presentation into markup and cannot be reused or overridden by a stylesheet's cascade as cleanly as a class can. ```html

Inline-styled warning text.

``` ## data-* Attributes Custom `data-*` attributes let you attach your own metadata to an element without breaking validation, for use by your own JavaScript or CSS attribute selectors. ```html ``` In JavaScript, these are read through the `dataset` property: `button.dataset.userId` returns `"482"`. ## Other Common Global Attributes - `title` - adds an advisory tooltip shown on hover. - `tabindex` - controls keyboard focus order. - `hidden` - hides the element entirely from rendering and assistive technology. - `lang` - overrides the document language for a specific element.

codeExamples.description: An element combining id, class, a data attribute, and a title tooltip
codeExamples.code:
<button
  id="save-btn"
  class="btn btn-primary"
  data-action="save-document"
  title="Save your changes">
  Save
</button>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a clickable button labeled 'Save'. Hovering it shows a native browser tooltip reading 'Save your changes'. CSS can target it via #save-btn or .btn-primary, and JavaScript can read button.dataset.action, which returns 'save-document'.

codeExamples.description: The hidden attribute removing an element from rendering entirely
codeExamples.code:
This paragraph is always visible.

This paragraph is completely removed from rendering and from assistive technology.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Only the first paragraph is visible on the page; the second paragraph takes up no space at all and is skipped entirely by screen readers, equivalent to applying display: none to it.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between `<strong>`/`<em>` and `<b>`/`<i>`?
interviewQuestions.answer:
`` and `` are **semantic** elements: they convey meaning about the text's importance or emphasis, which assistive technologies like screen readers can use to change intonation or flag importance to the user. `` and `` are purely **presentational**: they request bold or italic styling with no implied meaning. - `` = strong importance, seriousness, or urgency (often bold by default). - `` = stress emphasis that changes the meaning of a sentence (often italic by default). - `` = draws attention to text without conveying extra importance (e.g., keywords in a summary, product names). - `` = text in an alternate voice or mood, such as a technical term, a foreign phrase, or a ship's name - not emphasis. ```html

Warning: this action cannot be undone.

I did send the email yesterday.

The Titanic set sail in 1912.

``` In practice, most content calling for bold or italic *emphasis* should use ``/``; reach for ``/`` only when there truly is no additional semantic weight, just a stylistic convention.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A content team wants product keywords bolded throughout a catalog page purely for visual scanning, with no implication that any one keyword is more 'important' than another.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Using `<b>` and `<i>` purely because they are shorter to type, even when real emphasis or importance is intended; using `<strong>`/`<em>` purely for visual styling and then fighting their default bold/italic look with CSS instead of picking the semantically correct tag to begin with.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How would a screen reader typically announce text wrapped in `<strong>` versus `<b>`?
Is it ever acceptable to nest `<strong>` inside `<em>`, and what does that combination mean?

interviewQuestions.question: What are HTML void (empty) elements? Give several examples and explain why they cannot have a closing tag or children.
interviewQuestions.answer:
Void elements are HTML elements that can never have any content or children - they represent a single point of information and are inherently "empty" by the HTML specification, so they must not be given a closing tag. Common void elements include: - `
` - line break - `
` - thematic break (horizontal rule) - `` - image - `` - form control - `` - metadata - `` - external resource reference - `` - image map region - `` - media source for ``/`
interviewQuestions.scenario: A developer coming from a strict XML background writes `<input type="text"></input>` and the linter flags it as invalid markup.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Trying to put content between a void element's opening and a (non-existent) closing tag; assuming the self-closing slash is required in HTML5 (it is optional and purely stylistic); forgetting that void elements still accept attributes even though they take no children.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
Is `<script>` a void element? Why or why not?
How does the HTML parser recover when it encounters an unexpected closing tag for a void element?

interviewQuestions.question: What determines whether an element is rendered as 'block' or 'inline' by default, and how do global attributes and CSS interact with that default?
interviewQuestions.answer:
Every HTML element has a default CSS `display` value defined by the browser's built-in user-agent stylesheet, based on the element's category in the HTML specification, not by any rule hardcoded into the parser itself. For example, `
`, `

`, and `

`-`

` default to `display: block` (they start on a new line and stretch to fill available width), while ``, ``, and `` default to `display: inline` (they flow within a line of text and only take up the width of their content). This default is just a *starting point* - it can always be overridden with CSS, and doing so is common: a `` can be made `display: block`, or a `
    `'s `
  • ` items can be made `display: inline` to build a horizontal navigation bar. The HTML specification itself does not mandate visual rendering; browsers mandate it through their default stylesheets, which is why the exact rendering can occasionally differ in edge cases between browser engines, though all major engines agree on the common elements. Global attributes do not change an element's default `display` value, but they interact with layout in related ways: - The `hidden` attribute removes the element from rendering entirely (equivalent to `display: none`), overriding whatever display value would otherwise apply. - The `style` attribute can set `display` directly on that one element, taking the highest specificity short of `!important`. - `class`/`id` are used by external or embedded CSS to target and override the default display value at scale. Understanding this distinction - that "block vs inline" is a *stylistic* default rather than an intrinsic property of the tag - is important for building accessible, flexible layouts, since you should choose tags for their semantic meaning and use CSS to control their visual presentation independently.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A team builds a horizontal pill-style navigation menu using `<li>` elements and is confused why their CSS `display: inline-block` rule is necessary at all, since `<li>` normally stacks vertically.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Assuming display behavior is fixed by the HTML spec rather than by the browser's default stylesheet; using `<div>`-only markup and recreating block/inline behavior with CSS instead of picking semantically appropriate elements; forgetting that `hidden` overrides any CSS display value unless CSS explicitly re-enables it with `display` in a stylesheet rule, which is a common source of 'why won't hidden go away' bugs.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How would you make a `<span>` behave like a block-level box without changing the HTML tag?
What happens if both the `hidden` attribute and a CSS rule set `display: block` on the same element - which one wins?

topics.summary: Learn how to document HTML with comments and understand how browsers collapse whitespace when rendering text.

lessons.title: Writing HTML Comments
lessons.contentMarkdown:
Comments let you leave notes in your markup that browsers ignore completely when rendering the page. They are useful for documentation, temporarily disabling a block of markup during development, and leaving instructions for teammates. ## Syntax An HTML comment starts with ``. Everything between the two markers is ignored by the browser's renderer, though it is still downloaded and visible to anyone who views the page source - so comments are not a security mechanism and should never contain sensitive information like credentials or internal API details. ```html

Visible text.

``` ## Common Uses - **Documentation**: explaining why a particular piece of markup exists, especially for workarounds or browser-specific fixes. - **Temporarily disabling markup**: wrapping a block in a comment to hide it without deleting it, useful while debugging. - **Section labels**: marking the start and end of large, generated sections of a page, which is common in templating systems and CMS output. ```html

© 2026 Example Co.

``` ## Rules and Restrictions Comments cannot be nested - the first `-->` encountered closes the comment, even if it appears inside what looks like a nested comment. The text immediately after ``. In practice, simply avoid putting `--` anywhere inside a comment and you will never run into these edge cases.

codeExamples.description: Using comments to label sections and temporarily disable a block of markup
codeExamples.code:
Home About

Main page content.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders the 'Home' and 'About' navigation links followed by the main content paragraph; the promo banner div between the comment markers is completely invisible and not part of the rendered DOM.

lessons.title: How Browsers Collapse Whitespace
lessons.contentMarkdown:
A common surprise for HTML beginners is that writing extra spaces, tabs, or line breaks in your markup usually has no visible effect at all. Understanding why requires knowing HTML's default whitespace handling rules. ## The Default Behavior By default (the CSS `white-space: normal` behavior, which every element starts with), the browser collapses any sequence of one or more spaces, tabs, and newlines into a single space when rendering text. This means you are free to indent your HTML source for readability without affecting how it looks on screen. ```html

Hello, world!

``` This renders exactly the same as `

Hello, world!

` - as a single space-separated line of text - because the newlines and indentation inside the paragraph collapse into a single space. ## Preserving Whitespace Sometimes you genuinely need to preserve exact spacing and line breaks, for example when displaying source code or ASCII art. The `
` element tells the browser to render its contents exactly as written, including all whitespace and line breaks, typically in a monospace font.

```html

function greet() {
  console.log("Hello");
}


```

## Non-Breaking Spaces

When you need a single extra space that will not be collapsed - for example, to prevent a label and its value from wrapping onto separate lines - use the ` ` character entity. Unlike a regular space, ` ` is never collapsed and also prevents a line break at that exact point.

```html

Price: $9.99

```

## Why This Matters for Clean Code

Because whitespace collapses by default, you should never try to achieve visual spacing (like multiple blank lines between paragraphs) by typing extra spaces or blank lines in your HTML. That kind of spacing belongs in CSS, using properties like `margin` and `padding`, which are reliable and consistent across browsers.

codeExamples.description: Comparing default whitespace collapsing against <pre>, which preserves formatting exactly
codeExamples.code:
This paragraph has many extra spaces.

This     block    preserves
    every  single    space.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The paragraph renders as 'This paragraph has many extra spaces.' with all repeated spaces and line breaks collapsed to single spaces. The <pre> block renders in a monospace font exactly as typed, preserving every extra space and the line break in the middle of the text.

codeExamples.description: Using   to keep a number and its unit from wrapping onto separate lines
codeExamples.code: In stock: 42 units available at 12 Main Street.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders as 'In stock: 42 units available at 12 Main Street.' with normal-looking spacing, but the browser will never break a line between '42' and 'units', or within '12 Main Street', even if the surrounding text wraps onto multiple lines.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you write a comment in HTML, and can HTML comments be nested?
interviewQuestions.answer:
An HTML comment begins with ``; everything between the two markers is ignored during rendering. ```html

Visible content

``` HTML comments **cannot be nested**. If you write ` still outer -->`, the parser closes the comment at the *first* `-->` it encounters, so everything after that point (`still outer -->`) is treated as regular markup, not as part of the comment, which usually produces visibly broken output. Comments are also not hidden from users who view the page source - they are sent to the browser as plain text, just not rendered - so they must never contain secrets, internal URLs, or sensitive notes.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A developer wraps a large block of old markup in a comment to disable it temporarily, but that old markup itself already contained an HTML comment, and the page renders with unexpected visible text.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Assuming comments nest like in many programming languages; forgetting that the double-hyphen sequence `--` is restricted inside a comment body; putting sensitive data (API keys, internal notes) inside a comment, forgetting it is visible in view-source.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
What happens if a comment body contains the literal string `--` in the middle, not just at the very end?
How would you find and remove all commented-out markup from a large, generated HTML file?

interviewQuestions.question:
Why does `

Hello world

` render as just "Hello world" with single spaces, and how would you preserve the original spacing if you needed to?
interviewQuestions.answer:
By default, every HTML element uses the CSS whitespace behavior equivalent to `white-space: normal`. Under this rule, the browser collapses any run of one or more spaces, tabs, and newlines in the text content into a single rendered space, and also trims leading/trailing whitespace adjacent to element boundaries in most contexts. This is why indentation and line breaks in your source file are free to use for readability - they essentially never affect the rendered page. To preserve exact whitespace, you have two options: 1. **The `
` element** - renders its content exactly as written, including every space and line break, typically in monospace font. Best for code snippets or ASCII-art style content.

```html

  Hello    world  

```

2. **The ` ` (non-breaking space) entity** - inserts a literal space character that is never collapsed and also prevents a line-wrap at that position. Useful for small, targeted spacing needs, like keeping a number and its unit together.

```html

Hello    world

```

For larger structural spacing (gaps between paragraphs, sections, etc.), neither of these is the right tool - use CSS `margin` or `padding` instead, since that keeps presentation separate from content and is far easier to maintain.
interviewQuestions.scenario:
A developer pastes a pre-formatted ASCII table into a `

` tag expecting it to display as a neat grid, but it instead collapses onto a single line.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Trying to control layout spacing by typing extra spaces or blank lines in HTML source; using ` ` repeatedly as a substitute for CSS margin/padding; forgetting that `<pre>` content is rendered literally, including any accidental leading whitespace from code indentation.

interviewQuestions.question: How does the CSS `white-space` property interact with HTML's default whitespace collapsing, and what is the practical difference between its `normal`, `pre`, `pre-wrap`, and `nowrap` values?
interviewQuestions.answer:
HTML itself does not define whitespace-collapsing rules in the markup language - collapsing is actually governed by the CSS specification's text processing rules, applied through the `white-space` property, which every element receives a default value for via the browser's built-in stylesheet (`normal` for most elements, `pre` for `
` and similar preformatted contexts).

The relevant `white-space` values behave as follows:

- **`normal`** (the default for most elements): sequences of whitespace collapse to a single space; line breaks in the source are ignored; text wraps automatically to fit its container.
- **`pre`**: whitespace is preserved exactly as written, including multiple spaces and line breaks; text does **not** wrap automatically, so long lines overflow their container unless explicitly scrolled or clipped. This is the default applied to `
`.
- **`pre-wrap`**: whitespace is preserved exactly like `pre`, but long lines *do* wrap to fit the container, combining literal formatting with responsive layout. Useful for displaying user-submitted text (like a chat message or comment) that may contain meaningful line breaks and should still wrap on small screens.
- **`nowrap`**: whitespace collapses like `normal`, but automatic line wrapping is disabled - text stays on a single line and will overflow its container unless an explicit `
` is inserted or the overflow is handled with CSS (e.g., `text-overflow: ellipsis`).

Because this is governed by CSS rather than hardcoded HTML behavior, you can change any element's whitespace handling by applying `white-space` yourself. For example, applying `white-space: pre-wrap` to a `
` that renders user-generated content preserves the user's intentional line breaks without needing to convert every newline into a literal `
` tag server-side, and without losing responsive wrapping on narrow viewports.

This distinction matters in real applications: a chat UI, a code-diff viewer, and a plain marketing paragraph each want a different combination of "preserve my line breaks" and "please still wrap long lines," and `white-space` is the single property that controls both independently.
interviewQuestions.scenario:
A support ticket system displays user-submitted messages inside `
` elements; messages with intentional line breaks are collapsing onto one line, and the team wants to preserve line breaks without converting every newline character into an HTML `
` tag in the backend.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Believing whitespace collapsing is a fixed HTML parser behavior rather than a CSS default that can be overridden anywhere; confusing `pre` (no wrapping) with `pre-wrap` (wraps) and picking the wrong one for user-generated content, causing horizontal scrollbars; forgetting that changing `white-space` does not change HTML entity behavior like ` `, which remains non-breaking regardless of the property's value.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How would `white-space: pre-line` differ from `pre-wrap`?
How does the `word-break` or `overflow-wrap` CSS property interact with `white-space: pre-wrap` when a single 'word' is longer than its container?

lessons.title: Heading Hierarchy and Document Outline
lessons.contentMarkdown:
Headings do more than make text bigger - they form a hierarchical outline of your document that assistive technology, browser extensions, and search engines use to understand how your content is organized. ## One h1, Then Logical Nesting The modern best practice is to use exactly one `

` per page, describing the page's overall topic, and then nest `

` through `

` beneath it to represent sub-topics, without skipping levels. ```html

Complete Guide to Houseplants

Choosing a Plant

Low-Light Options

High-Light Options

Watering Schedules

Succulents

Tropical Plants

``` This creates an outline identical in structure to a table of contents: "Choosing a Plant" and "Watering Schedules" are both top-level sections (`

`), each with their own sub-sections (`

`). ## Why Skipping Levels Is a Problem Jumping from `

` straight to `

` because "it looked like the right font size" breaks the outline. Screen reader users frequently navigate a page heading-by-heading using a single keystroke, and an inconsistent hierarchy makes the page's structure confusing or outright misleading, even though sighted users looking only at font size might not notice anything wrong. ```html

Page Title

A Subsection

``` ## Headings Are Not a Styling Tool If you want large, bold text purely for visual effect with no structural meaning, that is a job for CSS (`font-size`, `font-weight`) applied to a `

` or ``, not for misusing a heading tag. Conversely, never shrink an `

` down with CSS just because a design calls for small text in a spot that is structurally still a genuine section heading - keep the tag matching the structure, and let CSS handle the visual size independently.

interviewQuestions.question: Why does the `alt` attribute matter on `` elements, and what should you put in it for a purely decorative image?
interviewQuestions.answer: The `alt` attribute provides a text alternative for an image, which is announced by screen readers in place of the image and displayed if the image fails to load. It is essential for users who cannot see the image, whether due to visual impairment, a slow connection, or a broken image URL. For a meaningful image - a photo, chart, icon that conveys information, or a logo - `alt` should describe the information or purpose the image serves in context, concisely: ```html ``` For a **purely decorative** image that adds no information (a background pattern, a visual spacer, a flourish beside a heading that already states the same thing in text), use an empty string, `alt=""`. This explicitly tells assistive technology to skip the image entirely, rather than reading out a filename or a redundant description. ```html ``` The one thing you should never do is omit the `alt` attribute altogether - in that case, many screen readers fall back to announcing the raw image filename (e.g., "IMG dash two zero three four dot jay peg"), which is a jarring, useless experience.
interviewQuestions.scenario: An e-commerce product page includes both a meaningful product photo and a small decorative divider graphic between sections, and the team needs to decide what alt text, if any, each one should have.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Omitting the alt attribute entirely rather than setting it to an empty string for decorative images; writing overly literal descriptions like 'image of a red button' instead of describing the image's purpose; stuffing alt text with keywords for SEO purposes, which degrades the experience for actual screen reader users.

interviewQuestions.question: How do screen readers use heading hierarchy to help users navigate a page, and what breaks if that hierarchy is inconsistent?
interviewQuestions.answer:
Screen readers build a navigable list of all headings on a page, typically accessible through a dedicated keyboard shortcut (for example, pressing "H" to jump to the next heading, or opening a rotor/headings list that shows the entire hierarchy at once, indented by level). This lets a user skip directly to the section they care about instead of listening to the entire page read out top to bottom. For this to work well, heading levels must be used consistently to reflect actual document structure: - Exactly one `

` per page describing its overall topic. - `

` for top-level sections under that topic. - `

` nested under the relevant `

`, and so on - never skipping a level purely because of how it looks visually. When hierarchy is inconsistent - for example, jumping from `

` straight to `

`, or using multiple unrelated `

`s - the generated outline becomes confusing or misleading. A user navigating by heading level might expect an `

` to be a minor sub-point of the nearest `

`, but if no `

` exists, they lose confidence in the structure and have to fall back to reading linearly, defeating the purpose of providing headings at all. ```html

``` The practical guideline: choose heading tags based on their position in the outline first, then adjust font size, weight, and spacing separately with CSS to match the visual design.

interviewQuestions.question: What landmark roles do semantic elements expose to assistive technology by default, and what happened to the HTML5 'outline algorithm' that `<section>`/`<article>` were originally supposed to support?
interviewQuestions.answer:
Several semantic HTML5 elements carry an implicit ARIA landmark role, exposed automatically in the accessibility tree without any extra `role` attribute:

- `<header>` (when not nested inside `<article>`/`<section>`) -> `banner`
- `<nav>` -> `navigation`
- `<main>` -> `main`
- `<footer>` (when not nested inside `<article>`/`<section>`) -> `contentinfo`
- `<aside>` -> `complementary`
- `<form>` (with an accessible name) -> `form`
- `<section>` (only when it has an accessible name, e.g. via `aria-label` or a heading referenced with `aria-labelledby`) -> `region`

Screen readers expose a "landmarks" list built from these roles, letting users jump directly between major page regions - this is a real, currently-supported accessibility feature, independent of any heading-based outline.

Separately, the original HTML5 specification proposed a **document outline algorithm**: the idea that nested `<section>` and `<article>` elements would implicitly create a new "outline level," so that an `<h1>` inside a nested `<section>` would be automatically treated as equivalent to a visually smaller heading, without the author needing to manually write `<h2>`, `<h3>`, etc. In practice, **no major browser ever implemented this algorithm**, and it was eventually removed from the HTML Living Standard. As a result, relying on nesting alone to imply heading level has never been reliable for real users on real assistive technology - authors must still manually choose the correct literal heading level (`<h1>`-`<h6>`) to reflect the true document structure, regardless of how deeply that heading is nested inside sectioning elements.

The practical implication: semantic sectioning elements are valuable for the landmark roles they expose and for conveying meaning to developers and tooling, but they do not relieve you of the responsibility to hand-author a correct, non-skipping heading hierarchy throughout the document.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A team builds a component library where a reusable 'Card' component automatically renders an <article> containing an <h1>, assuming nested sectioning content will make browsers 'demote' it visually and semantically wherever it's reused on a page that already has its own h1.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Relying on the (unimplemented) outline algorithm and assuming nested sectioning elements automatically adjust heading semantics; believing `<section>` always exposes a landmark role, when it only does so if it has an accessible name; forgetting that `<header>`/`<footer>` lose their banner/contentinfo roles once nested inside `<article>` or `<section>`, where they instead describe just that sub-section.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
Why does a <section> need an accessible name before it is exposed as a 'region' landmark, while <nav> and <main> are exposed unconditionally?
How would you design a reusable 'Card' component so it never accidentally emits a second <h1> on a page?

In other words: prefer `

``` ## When ARIA Is the Right Tool ARIA earns its keep for widgets with no native HTML equivalent: tab panels, accordions, comboboxes with autocomplete, tree views, toast/live-region notifications, and modal dialogs built before `` existed (the native `` element now covers much of that last case). ## aria-hidden `aria-hidden="true"` removes an element and its descendants from the accessibility tree entirely, without affecting visual rendering. It is commonly used on purely decorative icons that sit next to a text label, so the icon is not redundantly announced. ```html ``` Never apply `aria-hidden="true"` to an element that still contains focusable content (like a link or input) - doing so creates a focusable element that assistive technology cannot describe, which is a well-known accessibility trap. ## aria-label vs Visible Text Prefer real, visible text content whenever possible; reach for `aria-label` only when there is no visible text to associate, such as an icon-only button.

The problem it solves: native HTML has a fixed, relatively small set of interactive elements (`

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between `aria-label` and `aria-labelledby`, and when would you use each?
interviewQuestions.answer:
Both provide an **accessible name** for an element - the text a screen reader announces to identify it - but they get that text from different places. **`aria-label`** supplies the accessible name directly as a string value on the attribute itself. Use it when there is no suitable visible text already on the page to reuse, most commonly on icon-only controls. ```html ``` **`aria-labelledby`** points to the `id` of one or more *other* elements already on the page, and uses their text content as the accessible name (concatenating multiple ids' text if more than one is listed). Use it when visible text that should serve as the label already exists elsewhere, so you avoid duplicating the same string in two places. ```html

Delete this file?

This action cannot be undone.

``` A practical rule: if a visible heading, label, or text node that should serve as the name already exists, reference it with `aria-labelledby` rather than retyping the same string into `aria-label` - this keeps the two in sync automatically if the visible text ever changes, and avoids the maintenance risk of them drifting apart. Precedence note: when both are present on the same element, `aria-labelledby` takes priority over `aria-label`, which in turn takes priority over the element's own visible text content or `title` attribute.

interviewQuestions.question: Explain the "First Rule of ARIA" and describe a real situation where adding ARIA to a custom-built widget actually made it less accessible than using a native element would have.
interviewQuestions.answer:
The First Rule of ARIA, from the W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide, states: if a native HTML element or attribute already provides the semantics and behavior you need, use it instead of re-purposing a different element and patching in ARIA to compensate. In short: ARIA is a last resort for filling gaps in native HTML, not a first choice, and not a universal accessibility fix.

**Why misuse backfires**: ARIA roles and states only change what is reported in the accessibility tree. They do not grant keyboard focusability, do not wire up Enter/Space activation, do not add any default visual focus indicator, and do not make an element participate in form submission. If a developer adds `role="button"` to a `<div>` but forgets `tabindex="0"` and a `keydown` handler for Enter and Space, the result is actively worse than doing nothing: a screen reader now announces "button," raising the user's expectation that it behaves like a real button, but keyboard users (who may rely entirely on Tab and Enter, including many screen reader users) cannot actually reach or activate it at all. A real `<button>` would have given all of that for free, correctly, in every browser, with zero extra code.

**Concrete example**: a team builds a custom checkbox purely from a styled `<div role="checkbox">` to achieve a specific visual design the native `<input type="checkbox">` didn't support with their CSS approach. They add `aria-checked="false"` and toggle it on click with JavaScript, but overlook: (1) making it focusable via `tabindex="0"`, (2) toggling on Space key press (the native convention for checkboxes), and (3) ensuring the checked state participates in an actual `<form>` submission. The visual design now "looks" like a checkbox and is announced as one, but keyboard-only and screen-reader users cannot reliably toggle it, and the form silently fails to submit its value. A native `<input type="checkbox">`, restyled with CSS (which is almost always achievable with modern CSS, including the `appearance: none` approach and custom-drawn check-marks via `::before`/`::after` or `accent-color`), would have avoided every one of these problems while still meeting the visual requirement.

The broader lesson: ARIA is genuinely necessary for widgets with no native equivalent (tab panels, comboboxes, tree views, toast notifications), but every ARIA role you add is also an explicit promise to the user that you will manually reimplement all of the keyboard interaction, focus management, and state behavior that the role implies - a promise that is easy to under-deliver on.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A design team insists on a pixel-perfect custom checkbox that the native input's styling cannot achieve with the project's CSS constraints, and a developer reaches for role="checkbox" on a div without replicating native keyboard behavior, passing a visual QA review but failing an accessibility audit.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Assuming adding an ARIA role alone is sufficient without also replicating native keyboard interaction and focus management; underestimating how much free, correct, cross-browser behavior native elements provide; not testing custom widgets with an actual keyboard (no mouse) or a real screen reader before shipping.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
What specific keyboard interactions does the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide specify for a custom tab panel widget?
How far can you push a native <input type="checkbox"> with modern CSS before truly needing a fully custom, ARIA-driven implementation?

topics.title: Form Elements & the Form Tag
topics.summary: Learn how the form element collects and submits user input, and how to group and label controls accessibly.

lessons.title: Building a Basic Form
lessons.contentMarkdown:
The `<form>` element wraps a collection of input controls and defines how their values get submitted to a server.

## The form Element and Its Key Attributes

```html
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <input type="text" name="email" placeholder="you@example.com">
  <button type="submit">Subscribe</button>
</form>
```

- `action` - the URL the form data is sent to. If omitted, the form submits to the current page's URL.
- `method` - the HTTP method used, almost always `get` or `post`.

## GET vs POST at a Glance

- `method="get"` appends form data as a query string onto the URL (`?email=you%40example.com`). Suitable for searches and filters - requests that just retrieve data and are safe to bookmark or repeat.
- `method="post"` sends form data in the request body, invisible in the URL. Suitable for anything that creates, updates, or deletes data, or that includes sensitive information, since GET data is logged in browser history and server logs.

## Every Control Needs a name

Only form controls with a `name` attribute are included in the submitted data; the `name` becomes the key, and the control's value becomes the value.

```html
<input type="text" name="username">
```

Without `name`, a field's value is typed by the user but silently dropped from submission - a very common beginner bug.

## Buttons Inside a Form

- `<button type="submit">` (the default type inside a form) submits the form.
- `<button type="reset">` clears all fields back to their initial values.
- `<button type="button">` does nothing on its own - useful for attaching custom JavaScript behavior without triggering a submission.

```html
<form action="/search" method="get">
  <input type="search" name="q">
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>
```

codeExamples.description: A simple GET-based search form and a POST-based signup form
codeExamples.code:
<form action="/search" method="get">
  <input type="search" name="q" placeholder="Search the site">
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <input type="text" name="username" placeholder="Username">
  <input type="password" name="password" placeholder="Password">
  <button type="submit">Create Account</button>
</form>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a search box and button that, on submit, navigates to '/search?q=whatever-was-typed'. The signup form renders a username field, a masked password field, and a 'Create Account' button that submits both values in the POST request body rather than the URL.

lessons.title: Labels, Fieldsets, and Legends
lessons.contentMarkdown:
A form full of unlabeled inputs is unusable for screen reader users and frustrating for everyone else, since clicking near a field does nothing unless the label is properly associated with it.

## The label Element

`<label>` associates descriptive text with a form control in one of two ways:

**Explicit association** using `for`, matching the control's `id`:

```html
<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email">
```

**Implicit association** by wrapping the control inside the label:

```html
<label>
  Email address
  <input type="email" name="email">
</label>
```

Either approach lets users click or tap the label text to focus the associated control, and both are announced correctly by screen readers. The explicit `for`/`id` approach is generally preferred for its flexibility in layout, since the label and control don't need to be adjacent in the markup.

## fieldset and legend

`<fieldset>` groups a set of related controls, drawing a visual border around them by default, and `<legend>` provides a caption for that group - commonly used for radio button groups, checkbox groups, or logically related sections of a longer form.

```html
<fieldset>
  <legend>Preferred contact method</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="contact" value="email"> Email</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="contact" value="phone"> Phone</label>
</fieldset>
```

Screen readers announce the `<legend>` text as part of each control's accessible name within the group, so a user tabbing to the "Email" radio button hears something like "Preferred contact method, Email, radio button, not checked" - context that would otherwise be lost.

## Disabling an Entire Group

Setting `disabled` on a `<fieldset>` disables every form control nested inside it at once, which is convenient for sections that depend on an earlier choice (for example, graying out shipping options until a delivery method is chosen).

codeExamples.description: A fieldset grouping radio buttons, each properly associated with its label
codeExamples.code:
<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Preferred contact method</legend>
    <label for="contact-email">
      <input type="radio" id="contact-email" name="contact" value="email"> Email
    </label>
    <label for="contact-phone">
      <input type="radio" id="contact-phone" name="contact" value="phone"> Phone
    </label>
  </fieldset>
</form>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a bordered box titled 'Preferred contact method' containing two radio buttons labeled 'Email' and 'Phone'. Clicking either label text (not just the small radio circle) selects that option, and a screen reader announces both the legend and the label when each radio button receives focus.

codeExamples.description: An implicitly-associated label, wrapping the input directly, as an alternative to the for/id pattern
codeExamples.code:
<label>
  Email address
  <input type="email" name="email">
</label>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders the text 'Email address' immediately followed by an email input field. Clicking anywhere on the words 'Email address' moves keyboard focus into the input, exactly as if an explicit for/id pair had been used, without needing a matching id attribute at all.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the `for` attribute on a `<label>` element, and what happens if it's missing or incorrect?
interviewQuestions.answer:
The `for` attribute on `<label>` creates a programmatic association with a form control by matching the control's `id` attribute. This association provides two key benefits:

1. **Clickable target expansion** - clicking or tapping anywhere on the label text (not just the small input itself) moves focus to, or toggles, the associated control. This is especially important for small targets like checkboxes and radio buttons, and for users with limited motor precision.

2. **Accessible naming** - screen readers announce the label text as the control's accessible name when it receives focus, so a user knows what the field is for without needing to see it.

```html
<label for="newsletter">Subscribe to newsletter</label>
<input type="checkbox" id="newsletter" name="newsletter">
```

If `for` is missing, misspelled, or points to an `id` that doesn't exist anywhere on the page, the association silently fails: the text still displays visually, but clicking it does nothing, and a screen reader announces the input with no accessible name at all (or just reads "checkbox, not checked" with no indication of what it controls). This is a frequent, easy-to-miss accessibility bug, since the page looks completely correct to a sighted user testing only with a mouse.

An alternative that avoids the matching-id problem entirely is wrapping the control directly inside the `<label>` (implicit association), which works without any `for`/`id` pairing at all.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A QA tester notices that clicking directly on a checkbox toggles it, but clicking the descriptive text right next to it does nothing, even though visually they look connected.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Mismatched or duplicate id values across the page, since id must be unique; forgetting the for attribute altogether and relying only on visual adjacency, which conveys nothing to screen readers; wrapping multiple unrelated controls inside one label.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
What is the difference between explicit (for/id) and implicit (wrapped) label association?
Can a single label be associated with more than one form control?

interviewQuestions.question: What is the practical difference between `method="get"` and `method="post"` on a `<form>`, and how would you decide which to use?
interviewQuestions.answer:
The `method` attribute controls how the browser packages and sends form data in the resulting HTTP request.

**`method="get"`** (the default if omitted) appends the form's field names and values as a URL query string, and sends an HTTP GET request.

```html
<form action="/search" method="get">
  <input type="text" name="q">
</form>
<!-- Submitting "html forms" navigates to: /search?q=html+forms -->
```

Characteristics: the resulting URL is bookmarkable and shareable, it appears in browser history and server access logs, and it has practical length limits imposed by browsers and servers. It's appropriate for idempotent, read-only operations like search and filtering, where "submitting the same request twice" causes no harm and being linkable is actually a feature.

**`method="post"`** sends form data in the HTTP request body instead, as an HTTP POST request.

```html
<form action="/signup" method="post">
  <input type="password" name="password">
</form>
```

Characteristics: data does not appear in the URL, is not cached or stored in browser history the same way, and has no practical size limit in the same way GET does. It's the correct choice for anything that changes server state (creating an account, submitting a payment, deleting a resource) or that includes sensitive data like passwords, since a password sent via GET would end up logged in plaintext in server access logs and browser history.

The decision rule: if the action is read-only and safe to repeat or bookmark, use GET; if it changes data or carries sensitive information, use POST. Note that `method` only controls form submission - it has no bearing on how JavaScript-driven `fetch`/`XMLHttpRequest` requests are sent, which are configured independently.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A developer builds a login form using method="get" by accident, and after testing, notices the user's password appears in plain text in the browser's address bar and in the server's access logs.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Using GET for forms that change server-side state, making those actions repeatable by simply reloading or revisiting a bookmarked URL; using GET for sensitive data like passwords; assuming POST data is inherently encrypted or secure, when in reality HTTPS - not the method - is what protects data in transit.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
Does using method="post" alone make a form submission secure? What else is required?
What happens if a GET form's combined field data exceeds a browser's or server's URL length limit?

interviewQuestions.question: How does a form behave when it contains multiple submit buttons, and how can `formaction`, `formmethod`, and similar attributes change submission behavior per-button?
interviewQuestions.answer:
A `<form>` can contain more than one submit control (`<button type="submit">` or `<input type="submit">`), and browsers only submit the data associated with whichever one the user actually activated - specifically, that button's own `name`/`value` pair (if it has one) is included in the submitted data, while the other submit buttons' name/value pairs are excluded entirely, even though they're all inside the same form.

```html
<form action="/order" method="post">
  <input type="hidden" name="product_id" value="482">
  <button type="submit" name="action" value="buy-now">Buy Now</button>
  <button type="submit" name="action" value="add-to-cart">Add to Cart</button>
</form>
```

Here, clicking "Buy Now" submits `action=buy-now` along with `product_id=482`; clicking "Add to Cart" instead submits `action=add-to-cart`. The server reads the submitted `action` value to decide which code path to run, without needing two separate `<form>` elements or any JavaScript.

Beyond differentiating which button was pressed, each submit button can individually **override** the form's own submission attributes using matching `form*`-prefixed attributes:

- `formaction` - overrides the form's `action` URL for that specific button.
- `formmethod` - overrides the form's `method` for that button.
- `formenctype` - overrides the encoding type (relevant when submitting files via `multipart/form-data`).
- `formnovalidate` - skips the browser's built-in constraint validation for that specific submission, useful for a "Save as Draft" button that shouldn't be blocked by `required` fields meant only for final submission.
- `formtarget` - overrides where the response loads (e.g., a new tab via `_blank`).

```html
<form action="/publish" method="post">
  <input type="text" name="title" required>
  <button type="submit">Publish</button>
  <button type="submit" formaction="/save-draft" formnovalidate>Save as Draft</button>
</form>
```

This lets a single form element serve multiple distinct submission behaviors declaratively, in plain HTML, without JavaScript intercepting the submit event to redirect or reconfigure the request manually - useful both for simplicity and as a reliable fallback if JavaScript fails to load.
interviewQuestions.scenario: An article editor page needs both a 'Publish' button, which should enforce that a title is filled in, and a 'Save as Draft' button that should succeed even with an empty title, without duplicating the entire form or writing custom JavaScript submit handling.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Assuming all submit buttons' name/value pairs are always sent together; not realizing formnovalidate only affects that specific button's submission, not the form in general; forgetting that formaction/formmethod only apply when that specific button triggers the submission, not when the form is submitted by pressing Enter in a text field (which defaults to the form's first submit button's behavior in most browsers).
interviewQuestions.followUps:
What happens if a form is submitted by pressing Enter inside a text input, and the form has multiple submit buttons - which one's formaction, if any, applies?
How would formenctype matter differently for a form that includes a file upload input?

topics.title: Input Types & Attributes
topics.summary: Survey the modern HTML5 input types and the common attributes that control their default value, behavior, and user experience.

lessons.title: Modern Input Types
lessons.contentMarkdown:
The `type` attribute on `<input>` dramatically changes how a control looks, how it validates, and which on-screen keyboard mobile devices display. Choosing the right type is one of the highest-value, lowest-effort improvements you can make to a form.

## Text-Like Types

```html
<input type="text" name="fullname">
<input type="email" name="email">
<input type="tel" name="phone">
<input type="url" name="website">
<input type="search" name="q">
<input type="password" name="password">
```

- `email` triggers built-in format validation and shows an "@"-friendly keyboard on mobile.
- `tel` shows a numeric phone keypad on mobile but applies no format validation by default, since phone number formats vary globally - pair it with `pattern` if you need to enforce a specific format.
- `url` validates that the value looks like a well-formed URL.
- `search` is styled like a search box in some browsers (often with a clear "x" button) and has no extra validation.
- `password` masks typed characters and is never auto-filled with saved values from other sites.

## Numeric and Date/Time Types

```html
<input type="number" name="quantity" min="1" max="10">
<input type="range" name="volume" min="0" max="100">
<input type="date" name="birthday">
<input type="time" name="appointment">
<input type="month" name="billing-month">
<input type="week" name="delivery-week">
```

`number` and `range` both restrict input to numeric values, but render completely differently: `number` shows a text field with up/down stepper arrows, while `range` renders a draggable slider with no visible numeric readout by default. The date/time family (`date`, `time`, `month`, `week`, and `datetime-local`) delegates to the operating system's native date picker UI, giving users a familiar, accessible calendar widget for free.

## Selection Types

```html
<input type="checkbox" name="agree" value="yes">
<input type="radio" name="plan" value="basic">
<input type="color" name="favorite-color">
<input type="file" name="attachment">
```

`checkbox` allows multiple independent selections; `radio` controls sharing the same `name` form a mutually-exclusive group, where only one can be checked at a time. `color` opens a native color picker, and `file` opens the operating system's file browser dialog.

## Why This Matters Beyond Styling

Beyond the visual control, many of these types enable free built-in validation (covered in depth in the next topic) and better mobile ergonomics, purely by choosing the correct `type` value instead of defaulting everything to `type="text"`.

codeExamples.description: A short form using several modern input types for an event registration
codeExamples.code:
<form>
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>

  <label for="attendees">Number of attendees</label>
  <input type="number" id="attendees" name="attendees" min="1" max="8" value="1">

  <label for="event-date">Preferred date</label>
  <input type="date" id="event-date" name="event-date">

  <button type="submit">Register</button>
</form>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders an email field that shows an email-optimized keyboard on mobile and rejects submission if not a valid email format, a number field with up/down steppers constrained between 1 and 8, and a date field that opens the browser's native calendar picker when focused.

lessons.title: Useful Input Attributes
lessons.contentMarkdown:
Beyond `type`, a handful of attributes shape how an input behaves and how it interacts with the browser's autofill and accessibility features.

## placeholder vs value

```html
<input type="text" name="search" placeholder="Search products...">
<input type="text" name="country" value="United States">
```

`placeholder` shows faint hint text inside an empty field that disappears as soon as the user types; it is **not** submitted as data and should never be used as a replacement for a real `<label>`, since it vanishes the moment the field has content, leaving users without context. `value` sets the field's actual starting content, which the user can edit, and which *is* submitted if left unchanged.

## autocomplete

```html
<input type="email" name="email" autocomplete="email">
<input type="text" name="cc-number" autocomplete="cc-number">
```

`autocomplete` hints to the browser which category of saved data to suggest for autofill (email, shipping address, credit card number, etc.), using a standardized vocabulary of values. Setting it correctly meaningfully speeds up checkout and signup flows. Use `autocomplete="off"` sparingly - mainly for genuinely one-off fields - since disabling autofill broadly hurts usability.

## disabled vs readonly

```html
<input type="text" name="promo-code" value="WELCOME10" readonly>
<input type="text" name="referral-code" disabled>
```

Both prevent editing, but differ in two important ways:
- A `disabled` field's value is **not submitted** with the form at all; a `readonly` field's value **is submitted**.
- A `disabled` field cannot receive focus or be interacted with in any way; a `readonly` field can still be focused, selected, and copied, just not edited.

## list and datalist

```html
<input type="text" name="browser" list="browser-options">
<datalist id="browser-options">
  <option value="Chrome">
  <option value="Firefox">
  <option value="Safari">
</datalist>
```

Linking an input to a `<datalist>` via the `list` attribute provides a dropdown of suggestions while still allowing the user to type any free-form value - unlike `<select>`, which restricts input to only the listed options.

## autofocus and multiple

`autofocus` places the keyboard cursor in that field automatically when the page loads (use sparingly - it can be disorienting, especially for screen reader users, and only one element per page should have it). `multiple`, when added to `type="file"` or `type="email"`, allows selecting several files or entering several comma-separated email addresses respectively.

codeExamples.description: Demonstrating placeholder vs value, readonly vs disabled, and a datalist of suggestions
codeExamples.code:
<label for="coupon">Coupon code</label>
<input type="text" id="coupon" name="coupon" value="WELCOME10" readonly>

<label for="browser">Preferred browser</label>
<input type="text" id="browser" name="browser" list="browser-options" placeholder="Start typing...">
<datalist id="browser-options">
  <option value="Chrome">
  <option value="Firefox">
  <option value="Safari">
</datalist>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a coupon field pre-filled with 'WELCOME10' that cannot be edited but is still submitted with the form, and a text field showing faint 'Start typing...' hint text that, once focused, shows a native dropdown suggesting Chrome, Firefox, or Safari while still accepting any typed value.

codeExamples.description: Comparing disabled and readonly side by side to show the submission difference
codeExamples.code:
<form action="/update-profile" method="post">
  <input type="text" name="account-id" value="ACC-9921" readonly>
  <input type="text" name="legacy-field" value="unused" disabled>
  <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: On submission, the request body includes account-id=ACC-9921 because readonly fields are still submitted, but contains no legacy-field entry at all, because disabled fields are excluded from form submission entirely.

interviewQuestions.question: Name several HTML5 input types beyond `text` and explain what each one is best suited for.
interviewQuestions.answer:
HTML5 added many purpose-specific input types that improve validation and mobile usability compared to always using `type="text"`:

- **`email`** - for email addresses; triggers basic format validation and an "@"-friendly mobile keyboard.
- **`password`** - masks characters as they're typed and is excluded from browser autofill-across-sites suggestions by default.
- **`tel`** - for phone numbers; shows a numeric phone keypad on mobile, with no built-in format validation (formats vary too much globally).
- **`number`** - for numeric values; shows stepper arrows and can be constrained with `min`/`max`/`step`.
- **`date`**, **`time`**, **`month`**, **`week`**, **`datetime-local`** - open the operating system's native date/time picker.
- **`checkbox`** - independent on/off toggle; multiple can be checked at once.
- **`radio`** - mutually exclusive choice among controls sharing the same `name`.
- **`range`** - a draggable slider for a numeric value within a defined range.
- **`color`** - opens a native color picker, submitting a hex color string.
- **`file`** - opens a file-selection dialog for uploads.
- **`search`** - styled as a search box in some browsers, often with a built-in clear button.

```html
<input type="email" name="email" placeholder="you@example.com">
<input type="date" name="start-date">
```

Choosing the correct type is nearly free - it takes the same amount of markup as `type="text"` - but gains you built-in validation hints and a better-matched on-screen keyboard on mobile devices.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A mobile checkout form uses type="text" for every field, including the phone number and card expiry month, and users complain that typing numbers on their phone is unnecessarily slow and error-prone.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Defaulting every field to type="text" out of habit; using type="number" for things that are not really mathematical quantities, like phone numbers or credit card numbers, which can cause unwanted stepper arrows and locale-dependent formatting issues; forgetting that tel performs no format validation on its own.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
Why is type="number" generally discouraged for credit card numbers or phone numbers, even though they're made of digits?
How does type="date" behave differently across different browsers' native pickers?

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between the `placeholder` and `value` attributes on an `<input>`, and why shouldn't `placeholder` be used as a substitute for a `<label>`?
interviewQuestions.answer:
**`value`** sets the actual initial content of the field. It is a real, editable value that the user can modify, and whatever remains in the field (whether left as the default or edited) is submitted with the form.

**`placeholder`** displays faint hint text only while the field is empty; it disappears the instant the user types anything, is never submitted as form data, and does not pre-fill the field with an editable starting value.

```html
<input type="text" name="city" value="New York">
<!-- vs -->
<input type="text" name="city" placeholder="e.g. New York">
```

`placeholder` should never replace a real `<label>` for several concrete reasons:
1. It vanishes as soon as the user starts typing, so there is no persistent indication of what the field is once it has content - problematic for anyone who gets interrupted mid-form or needs to review their entries.
2. Many screen readers either don't announce placeholder text at all by default, or announce it inconsistently compared to a properly associated label.
3. Placeholder text typically has lower contrast than body text by design convention, which can make it hard to read for users with low vision.
4. It provides no click/tap target expansion the way a `<label for="...">` does.

```html
<label for="city">City</label>
<input type="text" id="city" name="city" placeholder="e.g. New York">
```

The correct pattern is to use both together: a real `<label>` for the persistent, accessible name, and `placeholder` only for a short supplementary example or format hint.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A sign-up form uses only placeholder text ('Full Name', 'Email', 'Password') with no visible <label> elements, to achieve a minimalist look, and an accessibility audit flags every field as having no accessible name once populated.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Treating placeholder as a lighter-weight replacement for label to save vertical space; assuming placeholder text is submitted with the form if the user doesn't change it; relying on placeholder's low-contrast styling as the only visual cue for a field's purpose.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How would you redesign a minimalist form to keep a clean visual look while still providing real, accessible labels?
What CSS techniques exist for visually hiding a label without hiding it from screen readers?

interviewQuestions.question: How does the `<datalist>` element work with an input's `list` attribute, and how does this combination differ in behavior and accessibility from a `<select>` dropdown?
interviewQuestions.answer:
`<datalist>` defines a set of predefined `<option>` suggestions that can be associated with a text-like `<input>` through the input's `list` attribute, which references the datalist's `id`.

```html
<label for="city">City</label>
<input type="text" id="city" name="city" list="city-options">
<datalist id="city-options">
  <option value="New York">
  <option value="Los Angeles">
  <option value="Chicago">
</datalist>
```

**Key behavioral differences from `<select>`:**

1. **Free text is still allowed.** With a datalist, the suggestions are just that - suggestions. The user can ignore every option and type any arbitrary string, and that arbitrary string is what gets submitted. A `<select>`, by contrast, constrains the submitted value strictly to one of its defined `<option>` values (ignoring the rare case of a `<select>` with no options matching, which simply submits nothing useful).

2. **Filtering as you type.** Most browsers automatically filter the suggestion list to match what has been typed so far, behaving like a lightweight autocomplete, whereas a native `<select>` shows its full fixed list every time it's opened (though some browsers do incremental type-to-jump within an open select).

3. **Styling and rendering control.** The suggestion dropdown for a datalist is rendered entirely by the browser and cannot be styled with CSS - the degree of visual customization available for a `<select>`'s own trigger button is also limited, but the two render quite differently across browsers, and datalist's suggestion popup is generally the less consistent of the two across engines.

4. **Accessibility support is uneven.** Native `<select>` has extremely mature, consistent screen reader and keyboard support across virtually all browsers and assistive technology combinations. `<datalist>` support, while present in all modern browsers, has historically had more inconsistencies in exactly how (and whether) the suggestion list is announced by different screen reader and browser pairings, so it is worth explicitly testing with your target assistive technology if datalist is central to a critical workflow.

**When to choose which:** use `<select>` when the value must be constrained to one of a fixed set of options (e.g., choosing a country from an exhaustive, pre-agreed list). Use `<input list="...">` with `<datalist>` when you want to speed up data entry with suggestions while still allowing values outside the list (e.g., a "tags" field, or a city name field where you can't realistically enumerate every possible city).
interviewQuestions.scenario: A job-posting form has a 'Skill' field where the product team wants to suggest common skills (JavaScript, Python, SQL) to encourage consistency, but also needs to allow niche or newly-emerging skills that aren't in any predefined list.
