interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Assuming datalist restricts input the same way select does; not testing datalist suggestion behavior with real screen readers before relying on it for a critical form field; expecting consistent visual styling of the suggestion dropdown across different browsers, which is not guaranteed.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How would server-side validation need to differ between a select-backed field and a datalist-backed field, given that one is constrained and the other is not?
Can a datalist's suggestions be populated or filtered dynamically via JavaScript based on what the user has typed so far?

topics.title: Client-side Validation Attributes
topics.summary: Use built-in HTML5 constraint attributes like required, pattern, min, and max to validate form input before it ever reaches the server.

lessons.title: Required, Pattern, and Length Constraints
lessons.contentMarkdown:
HTML5 includes a built-in Constraint Validation API that lets the browser block form submission and show a native error message when a field's value doesn't meet certain rules - all without writing a single line of JavaScript.

## required

The `required` attribute marks a field as mandatory. If the user tries to submit the form while it is empty, the browser blocks submission and shows a native validation bubble pointing at the field.

```html
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
```

## pattern

The `pattern` attribute takes a JavaScript-flavored regular expression (without delimiters) that the field's value must fully match. It only applies to certain text-like input types (`text`, `search`, `url`, `tel`, `email`, `password`).

```html
<label for="zip">ZIP code</label>
<input type="text" id="zip" name="zip" pattern="[0-9]{5}" title="Enter a 5-digit ZIP code">
```

The `pattern` attribute is matched against the *entire* value (as if wrapped in `^...$`), not just a substring. Always pair `pattern` with a `title` attribute - many browsers display the `title` text as part of the validation error message, explaining what format is expected.

## minlength and maxlength

```html
<label for="username">Username</label>
<input type="text" id="username" name="username" minlength="3" maxlength="20">
```

`minlength` blocks submission if fewer characters are entered than specified; `maxlength` prevents the user from typing *beyond* the limit in the first place (it is enforced at input time, not just submission time).

## Why This Isn't Enough on Its Own

Client-side validation is a UX convenience - it gives instant feedback without a round trip to the server. But it is trivial to bypass (disabling JavaScript doesn't even matter here, since it's native browser behavior - but a user can still submit directly via a tool like curl, or edit the DOM with devtools). Every one of these constraints must be duplicated with real server-side validation before trusting the data.

codeExamples.description: A signup form combining required, pattern, and length constraints with helpful validation messages
codeExamples.code:
<form>
  <label for="username">Username</label>
  <input type="text" id="username" name="username" required minlength="3" maxlength="20">

  <label for="zip">ZIP code</label>
  <input type="text" id="zip" name="zip" pattern="[0-9]{5}" title="Enter a 5-digit ZIP code" required>

  <button type="submit">Create Account</button>
</form>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: If the username is left empty, too short, or the ZIP code doesn't match exactly five digits, clicking 'Create Account' is blocked and the browser shows a native tooltip-style error message next to the offending field (the ZIP field's message includes 'Enter a 5-digit ZIP code' from the title attribute) instead of submitting the form.

lessons.title: Min, Max, Step, and Custom Validity

codeExamples.description: A numeric quantity field constrained with min/max/step, plus CSS styling based on validity state
codeExamples.code:
<style>
  input:invalid { border: 2px solid crimson; }
  input:valid { border: 2px solid seagreen; }
</style>

<label for="quantity">Quantity (multiples of 5, 5-50)</label>
<input type="number" id="quantity" name="quantity" min="5" max="50" step="5" value="5">
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a number input with a green border while its value is 5, 10, 15, ... up to 50; typing a value like 7 or 53 turns the border crimson-red because it falls outside the allowed range or doesn't align to the step of 5, and the browser blocks form submission until the value is corrected.

codeExamples.description: A date input constrained to a specific booking window using min and max
codeExamples.code:
<label for="checkin">Check-in date</label>
<input type="date" id="checkin" name="checkin" min="2026-06-01" max="2026-08-31">
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Opens the browser's native date picker; dates before June 1, 2026 or after August 31, 2026 are either disabled/grayed out in the picker or rejected as invalid if typed manually, blocking form submission until a date within the allowed window is chosen.

interviewQuestions.question: What does the `required` attribute do on a form field, and does it guarantee the data is actually valid by the time it reaches the server?
interviewQuestions.answer:
The `required` attribute marks a form control as mandatory. When a form is submitted, the browser runs its built-in Constraint Validation check: if any `required` field is empty (or, for checkboxes, unchecked; for radio groups, none selected), the browser blocks the submission entirely and displays a native inline error message pointing at the first invalid field, without any network request being made.

```html
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
```

However, `required` (and every other HTML5 validation attribute) is a **client-side, UX-level convenience only**. It does not guarantee the server ever receives valid data, because:

1. A user can disable JavaScript - irrelevant here, since this validation is native browser behavior, not JavaScript, but:
2. A user can submit a request directly to the server using tools like curl, Postman, or by scripting an HTTP request, completely bypassing the browser's form and its validation attributes.
3. A user can open devtools and simply remove the `required` attribute from the live DOM before submitting.

Because of this, every constraint expressed with `required`, `pattern`, `min`/`max`, etc. on the client **must be duplicated with real validation on the server**, which is the only validation that can actually be trusted to protect data integrity and security.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A backend API endpoint trusts that because the frontend form marks the 'email' field as required, every request it receives will always include a non-empty email value, and it crashes with a null-reference error when a request arrives without one.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Treating client-side required/pattern validation as a substitute for server-side validation; assuming JavaScript must be disabled for a user to bypass HTML validation, when a direct HTTP request bypasses it just as easily; forgetting that required on a checkbox means it must be checked, not merely present in the DOM.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How would you test that your server-side validation actually rejects a request that skips the HTML form entirely?
What happens to a required radio-button group if none of the radios share the exact same name attribute?

interviewQuestions.question: How does the `pattern` attribute work, and what are its limitations compared to writing full custom validation in JavaScript?
interviewQuestions.answer:
`pattern` accepts a JavaScript-flavored regular expression (written without the surrounding slashes or delimiters) that an input's value must match *in full* in order to be considered valid - the browser implicitly anchors the pattern with `^` and `$`, so a partial match anywhere in the string is not sufficient.

```html
<label for="phone">Phone (format: 123-456-7890)</label>
<input type="text" id="phone" name="phone" pattern="\d{3}-\d{3}-\d{4}" title="Format: 123-456-7890">
```

It only applies to certain text-like input types - `text`, `search`, `url`, `tel`, `email`, and `password` - and has no effect on types like `number` or `date`, which have their own numeric/date-specific constraints (`min`/`max`/`step`) instead.

**Key limitations compared to custom JavaScript validation:**

1. **No cross-field logic.** `pattern` can only validate a single field's own value in isolation; it cannot express rules like "this field must equal another field's value" (e.g., password confirmation) or "this field is required only if another checkbox is checked."
2. **No asynchronous checks.** It cannot query a server to check, for example, whether a username is already taken.
3. **Regex flavor differences are subtle.** The pattern attribute uses the same regex engine as JavaScript's `RegExp`, but some developers accidentally include delimiters (`/.../ `) or flags, which are not valid in the attribute value and will cause the pattern to be ignored or throw a console warning.
4. **Error message quality.** The default browser validation message for a failed pattern match is generic; pairing it with a `title` attribute improves this somewhat, but you have no control over exact wording or styling across different browsers, unlike a fully custom JavaScript-driven error UI.

For straightforward format checks (ZIP codes, simple ID formats), `pattern` is a lightweight, zero-dependency solution. For cross-field rules, async checks, or fully custom error presentation, JavaScript (often combined with `setCustomValidity()` to still participate in native form-blocking behavior) is necessary.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A checkout form needs to validate that a promo code field matches a specific alphanumeric format, and separately needs to confirm that a 'confirm email' field exactly matches the original 'email' field before allowing submission.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Writing a pattern with literal slashes or regex flags copied directly from JavaScript source code, which is invalid in the attribute; forgetting that pattern requires a full match, so prefixing/suffixing wildcards like .* are sometimes mistakenly thought necessary when they're not, or are needed when partial matching really is intended; not providing a title attribute, leaving users with a vague, unhelpful default error message.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How would you implement the 'confirm email must match email' rule using HTML attributes and a small amount of JavaScript together?
What happens if a pattern attribute contains an actually invalid regular expression - does the browser silently ignore it, or treat the field as always invalid?

interviewQuestions.question: Explain how `setCustomValidity()` and the `:invalid`/`:valid` CSS pseudo-classes fit into the broader HTML5 Constraint Validation API, and why none of this removes the need for server-side validation.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A security review of a web application finds that an API endpoint accepts and stores a negative 'quantity' value even though the corresponding HTML form field has min="1", because the review team sent the request directly rather than through the browser's form.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Treating a green :valid-styled field, or a successful client-side setCustomValidity check, as proof that the data is safe to trust server-side; building complex custom-validity logic in JavaScript without ever implementing the equivalent check in the backend; assuming constraint validation CSS pseudo-classes reflect server-confirmed correctness rather than purely local, client-side state.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How would you architect shared validation rules (e.g., a regex pattern) so the same rule is enforced identically on both the client and the server, avoiding duplication drift?
What JavaScript properties are available on an input's validity object besides a boolean valid/invalid flag (e.g., valueMissing, patternMismatch, rangeOverflow)?

topics.title: Images & the Picture Element
topics.summary: Learn how to embed images responsively with img, srcset, and sizes, and how picture enables true art direction.

lessons.title: The img Element and Responsive Images
lessons.contentMarkdown: The `` element embeds an image into a page. Its two required pieces of information are where the image comes from and what it means to users who cannot see it. ## The Basics ```html ``` - `src` - the image URL. - `alt` - the text alternative, required for accessibility (see the Semantic HTML category for a full discussion of writing good alt text). - `width` and `height` - the image's intrinsic pixel dimensions. Specifying both (even when the final display size is controlled by CSS) lets the browser reserve the correct amount of space before the image finishes downloading, preventing the rest of the page from jumping around as images load in - a key factor in the Cumulative Layout Shift performance metric. ## Serving Different Resolutions with srcset Modern devices have wildly different pixel densities and viewport widths. Sending the same large image to every device wastes bandwidth on small screens. The `srcset` attribute lets the browser choose the most appropriate image file from a list of candidates. ```html ``` - Each entry in `srcset` pairs a URL with a width descriptor (`400w` means "this file is 400 pixels wide"). - `sizes` tells the browser how much of the viewport width the image will actually occupy at different breakpoints, so it can calculate which candidate file best matches the image's real rendered size on that specific device. - `src` remains as a fallback for browsers that don't support `srcset`. The browser - not the server, and not a JavaScript library - decides which file to download, based on the device's actual screen size and pixel density, which is both more efficient and more reliable than User-Agent sniffing. ## loading="lazy" ```html ``` Setting `loading="lazy"` defers loading an off-screen image until the user scrolls near it, improving initial page load performance - but avoid it on images visible immediately in the viewport (like a hero banner), since deferring those can actually slow down perceived load time.

codeExamples.description: A responsive image using srcset and sizes, with lazy loading and explicit dimensions
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders an image that fills the available width. On a narrow phone screen the browser downloads hero-400w.jpg; on a desktop monitor it downloads hero-1600w.jpg, automatically selecting whichever file best matches the image's actual rendered size and the screen's pixel density. Because loading="lazy" is set, the browser skips downloading it entirely until the user scrolls it near the viewport.

lessons.title: The picture Element for Art Direction
lessons.contentMarkdown: `srcset` lets the browser choose a different-sized version of the *same image*. Sometimes, though, you need to swap in a genuinely *different* image or crop at different breakpoints - for example, a wide landscape crop on desktop and a tighter portrait crop on mobile. This is called **art direction**, and it requires ``. ## Structure ```html ``` `` wraps one or more `` elements followed by exactly one required ``. The browser evaluates each ``'s `media` condition in order and uses the first one that matches; if none match, it falls back to the ``. The `` inside is mandatory, serves as the ultimate fallback, and is also what actually renders - the `` elements never render anything by themselves. ## Serving Modern Image Formats with Fallbacks `` is also the standard way to offer a modern, smaller image format (like AVIF or WebP) while gracefully falling back to a universally-supported format like JPEG for older browsers. ```html ``` Here, `type` rather than `media` is used as the selection condition: the browser picks the first `` whose declared MIME type it actually knows how to decode, skipping formats it doesn't support, and only falling through to the plain `` JPEG if neither AVIF nor WebP is supported. ## picture vs srcset: Choosing the Right Tool - Use `srcset`/`sizes` on a plain `` when you're serving the *same* image content at different resolutions (resolution switching). - Use `` when you need to serve genuinely *different* image content - a different crop, aspect ratio, or file format - depending on viewport size or browser support (art direction and format negotiation). They can also be combined: each `` inside a `` can itself carry its own `srcset` with multiple width descriptors, handling both concerns at once.

codeExamples.description: Art direction: a tighter portrait crop on narrow screens, a wide crop on larger screens, with a universal fallback
codeExamples.expectedOutput: On a phone-sized viewport (600px or narrower), the browser downloads and displays summit-portrait.jpg, a tighter crop suited to a narrow screen. On a wider viewport, it displays summit-wide.jpg, a more panoramic crop. If a browser somehow fails to support picture/source at all, it falls back to rendering the img element's summit-wide.jpg directly.

codeExamples.description: Serving a modern AVIF/WebP format with a universal JPEG fallback using type-based source selection
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A browser that can decode AVIF downloads and displays produce.avif (the smallest file); a browser that supports WebP but not AVIF downloads produce.webp instead; a browser supporting neither falls back to displaying the universally-compatible produce.jpg.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the `alt` attribute on ``, and what happens when an image fails to load?
interviewQuestions.answer: The `alt` attribute provides a text alternative describing the image's content or purpose. It serves several roles: 1. **Accessibility** - screen readers announce the `alt` text instead of (or in addition to describing) the image, so users who cannot see it still receive the information or function it conveys. 2. **Broken image fallback** - if the image file fails to load (bad URL, network failure, blocked request), most browsers display the `alt` text in place of the broken image icon. 3. **SEO and content indexing** - search engines use `alt` text to understand what an image depicts, since they cannot "see" the pixels the way a human can. ```html ``` For purely decorative images that convey no information (so neither of the above purposes applies), use an empty `alt=""` rather than omitting the attribute - this explicitly signals to screen readers to skip the image, instead of falling back to announcing the raw filename, which is a confusing experience for the listener.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A company's marketing site experiences a CDN outage, and visitors on a slow connection see several broken image icons on the homepage with no indication of what was supposed to be there.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Omitting alt entirely instead of using an empty string for decorative images; writing alt text that's redundant with adjacent visible caption text; using meaningless filler text like 'image' or the literal filename as the alt value.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How does a screen reader behave differently when alt is missing versus when it is explicitly set to an empty string?
Should alt text ever be identical to a figcaption describing the same image?

interviewQuestions.question: How do the `srcset` and `sizes` attributes work together to implement responsive images, and why is `sizes` necessary even when `srcset` already lists each candidate's width?
interviewQuestions.answer: `srcset` provides the browser with a list of candidate image files, each tagged with a width descriptor describing that file's actual intrinsic pixel width. ```html ``` Knowing each file's width alone is not enough for the browser to pick the right one - it also needs to know how large the image will actually be *displayed* on the page, which depends on your CSS layout, not just the viewport width. That's what `sizes` provides: a list of media-condition/length pairs describing the rendered display width of the image at different breakpoints. In the example above, `sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 50vw"` tells the browser: "on viewports 600px wide or narrower, this image will render at 100% of the viewport width; otherwise, it will render at 50% of the viewport width." Combining that rendered-size information with the device's pixel density (e.g., a 2x "Retina" display needs roughly twice the pixel width for the same crisp physical size), the browser calculates the ideal file to request from the `srcset` list and downloads only that one. Without `sizes`, the browser has no idea how large the image will actually appear, so it falls back to assuming 100vw for every image, which can cause it to pick an unnecessarily large (or, in some layouts, too small) candidate file - undermining the whole purpose of providing multiple candidates in the first place. The `src` attribute remains important as a fallback for any browser that doesn't understand `srcset`/`sizes`, and functions as effectively one more (unlabeled) candidate for older but still srcset-aware browsers in certain fallback scenarios.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A product gallery page serves a 2000px-wide image file to every visitor, even those on small mobile screens on cellular connections, resulting in unnecessarily slow page loads and high data usage.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Adding srcset but omitting sizes, assuming the browser can infer rendered size purely from CSS without being told explicitly; providing width descriptors (100w, 200w) that don't match the actual file's real pixel width; assuming srcset lets you serve genuinely different cropped images (that is picture's job, not srcset's).
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How does srcset behave differently when using pixel-density descriptors (1x, 2x) instead of width descriptors (400w, 800w)?
Can an img element use both srcset width descriptors and a sizes attribute inside a CSS Grid or Flexbox layout where the image's rendered width changes based on sibling content?

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference in purpose between `srcset` on a plain `` and using the `` element, and walk through a concrete scenario where only `` can solve the problem?
interviewQuestions.answer: `srcset` (used directly on ``, with or without `sizes`) solves **resolution switching**: it lets the browser choose among several files that all contain the *same image content*, differing only in pixel dimensions or file size, picking whichever is the best match for the current viewport size and device pixel density. The browser's own algorithm decides which file to fetch; the author has no direct control over exactly which breakpoint maps to which file beyond providing `sizes` hints. `` solves two problems `srcset` alone cannot: 1. **Art direction** - serving genuinely *different image content* (different crop, aspect ratio, or framing) at different viewport sizes, using explicit `media` conditions on each `` that the author fully controls. 2. **Format negotiation** - serving a modern, smaller format (AVIF, WebP) to browsers that support decoding it, with a graceful fallback to a universal format (JPEG/PNG) for ones that don't, using the `type` attribute on each ``. **Concrete art-direction scenario**: a photo of a person standing at the edge of a mountain cliff, shot as a wide landscape photo. On a desktop, the wide framing, showing the dramatic scale of the cliff and valley, looks great. On a narrow mobile viewport, that same wide image - scaled down to fit a narrow column - shrinks the person down to a nearly invisible speck, losing the entire point of the photo. Simply serving a smaller *resolution* of the same wide crop (which is all `srcset` can do) does not fix this; you need an entirely different, tighter *crop* - typically a portrait-oriented close-up on the person - for narrow viewports. ```html ``` No combination of `srcset` width descriptors on a single `` can switch between two different *crops* of the same scene - `srcset` candidates are expected to be the same image content, just resized, since the browser may pick any of them based on pixel density alone, with no guarantee of which viewport width triggered the choice. ``'s `media`-conditioned `` elements give the author deterministic, explicit control over exactly which image shows at exactly which breakpoint, which is precisely the guarantee art direction requires. In practice, the two techniques are frequently combined: each `` inside a `` can itself include a `srcset` with multiple width descriptors, so a given crop is also offered at multiple resolutions for different pixel densities within that same breakpoint.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A travel magazine's hero photo looks dramatic on desktop as a wide panoramic shot, but on mobile the same image scaled down makes the article's subject nearly impossible to see, and simply serving a smaller file of the same crop does not solve the framing problem.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Trying to solve an art-direction problem by only adding more srcset width candidates, which cannot change the crop or framing, only the resolution; forgetting the mandatory fallback img inside picture, without which nothing renders if no source matches; ordering type-based source elements incorrectly, causing a less-preferred format to be selected before a more modern one.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
In what order should AVIF, WebP, and JPEG source elements be listed inside a picture element, and why does order matter for type-based selection?
How would you combine art-direction source elements (using media) with format-negotiation source elements (using type) in the same picture block?

topics.title: Audio & Video Elements
topics.summary: Embed native audio and video playback with controls, multiple source formats, and accessible caption tracks.

lessons.title: Embedding Audio
lessons.contentMarkdown:
The `<audio>` element plays sound files directly in the browser with a native player UI, with no plugins or third-party players required.

## Basic Usage

```html
<audio controls src="podcast-episode-12.mp3">
  Your browser does not support the audio element.
</audio>
```

- `controls` displays the browser's built-in play/pause, seek bar, volume, and (in most browsers) download/playback-speed controls. Without `controls`, the element plays nothing visible at all unless scripted via JavaScript, so almost every public-facing audio element should include it.
- The fallback text between the opening and closing tags is only shown by extremely old browsers that don't recognize `<audio>` at all; it is effectively dead code in any modern context, but remains valid, harmless markup to include.

## Multiple Source Formats

Not every browser supports every audio codec equally. Providing multiple `<source>` elements lets the browser pick whichever format it can actually play.

```html
<audio controls>
  <source src="episode-12.ogg" type="audio/ogg">
  <source src="episode-12.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
  Your browser does not support the audio element.
</audio>
```

The browser tries each `<source>` in order and uses the first one whose `type` it supports decoding, skipping the rest. MP3 (`audio/mpeg`) has near-universal support today, so a single MP3 source is often sufficient for most projects, but OGG/Opus is still a useful additional option for certain contexts.

## Other Useful Attributes

```html
<audio controls loop preload="metadata" src="background-music.mp3"></audio>
```

- `loop` restarts playback automatically when it finishes.
- `preload` hints how much to download in advance: `none` (don't preload), `metadata` (just load duration/dimensions), or `auto` (let the browser decide, often loading the whole file).
- `autoplay` starts playback immediately without user interaction - modern browsers heavily restrict this, generally requiring the audio to also be `muted` or for the user to have previously interacted with the site, specifically to prevent unwanted noise from autoplaying ads and videos.

codeExamples.description: An audio player offering two formats with fallback text for unsupported browsers
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders the browser's native audio player with play/pause, a seek bar, and a volume control. The browser downloads only the file duration/metadata up front (not the full audio) until playback is started, and plays whichever of the two source formats it supports, trying OGG first.

lessons.title: Embedding Video with Multiple Sources and Tracks
lessons.contentMarkdown: `

codeExamples.description: A video player with two source formats, English captions on by default, and a poster thumbnail
codeExamples.code:
<video controls width="640" height="360" poster="tutorial-thumb.jpg">
  <source src="tutorial.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="tutorial.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  <track src="captions-en.vtt" kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  Your browser does not support the video element.
</video>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a 640x360 video player showing the thumbnail image before playback begins, with native play/pause/seek/volume/fullscreen controls. English captions display automatically over the video once played, and can be toggled off via the player's captions button; the browser loads whichever of the WebM or MP4 sources it can decode.

codeExamples.description: A muted, looping, inline background video with no visible controls, suitable for a decorative hero section
codeExamples.code:
<video autoplay muted loop playsinline width="1280" height="720">
  <source src="background-loop.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="background-loop.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The video begins playing automatically without sound as soon as the page loads (browsers allow this specifically because muted is set), loops continuously, and plays inline within the page layout on mobile Safari instead of forcing fullscreen, with no visible play/pause controls since controls was omitted.

interviewQuestions.question: What does the `controls` attribute do on `<audio>` and `<video>` elements, and what happens if you forget it?
interviewQuestions.answer:
The `controls` attribute tells the browser to display its built-in playback UI for the element: play/pause button, a seek/progress bar, a volume control, and, for `<video>`, a fullscreen toggle and (in most browsers) a captions button if caption tracks are present.

```html
<video controls src="demo.mp4" width="640" height="360"></video>
```

If `controls` is omitted, the element renders with **no visible interface at all** - for `<audio>`, this usually means nothing is displayed on the page whatsoever, and the file never plays unless a script explicitly calls its `.play()` method. For `<video>`, the video frame (or a blank/black box) is still visible at the specified width/height, but there is no way for the user to start, pause, or seek through it without custom JavaScript.

This matters for any content meant to be played by the end user through direct interaction: without `controls`, the media is effectively unusable for a typical visitor, unless the page supplies a fully custom-built playback UI driven by the HTMLMediaElement JavaScript API (`play()`, `pause()`, `currentTime`, and related properties/events) as a replacement for the native controls.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A developer embeds a podcast episode with <audio src="episode.mp3"></audio> and is confused why nothing appears on the page at all, even though the network tab shows the file downloading successfully.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Forgetting controls and assuming the element is broken, rather than realizing it's rendering with no UI by design; adding controls but also autoplay without muted, which many browsers will block anyway, leading to confusion about why playback doesn't start; building a custom play button with JavaScript while leaving controls on as well, resulting in two separate, possibly conflicting playback UIs.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
What JavaScript methods and properties would you use to build a fully custom audio player UI instead of relying on the native controls attribute?
Why do most browsers require muted alongside autoplay in order to allow automatic playback?

interviewQuestions.question: Why would you provide multiple `<source>` elements inside a single `<video>` or `<audio>` tag instead of just one `src` attribute?
interviewQuestions.answer:
Different browsers support different audio/video codecs and container formats, for a mix of historical, licensing, and technical reasons - there is no single video or audio format with universal support across every browser and version. Providing multiple `<source>` elements lets you offer the same media content encoded in several different formats, and the browser automatically picks and downloads only the first one it can actually decode, skipping the rest.

```html
<video controls width="640" height="360">
  <source src="demo.webm" type="video/webm">
  <source src="demo.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  Your browser does not support the video element.
</video>
```

The browser evaluates each `<source>`'s `type` attribute in the order they're listed and commits to the first one it supports - it does not download and test multiple files to see which "works best," so ordering by your own preference (e.g., listing a more efficient format like WebM before a more universally compatible MP4 fallback) is meaningful.

Using a single `src` attribute directly on `<video>`/`<audio>` instead only works reliably if you are confident every target browser supports that one specific format - which, for video in particular, is risky without checking current browser support data, since MP4 (H.264) has the broadest support today but WebM and other formats can offer better compression for certain content. For audio, MP3 support is now close to universal, which is why many projects get away with a single MP3 `src` and skip the multiple-`<source>` pattern entirely for audio, even though it's still provided as an option.

The fallback text between the opening and closing tags only displays in the rare case that the browser doesn't understand the element or any of the provided sources at all.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A video tutorial fails to play for a subset of users on an older browser, while working fine for the majority, because the project only ever provided a single MP4 source and that browser's decoder lacks support for the specific encoding profile used.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Assuming one video format has truly universal support and skipping fallback sources entirely; listing sources in an arbitrary order rather than preference order, since the browser commits to the first supported type it encounters; forgetting that the type attribute on source should match the actual file's container/codec, since a mismatched or missing type can cause the browser to skip a source it could have otherwise played.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How does the browser decide between two source elements if both have type attributes it technically supports, but with different quality trade-offs?
What is the practical difference between the type attribute on a video source and inspecting the actual file bytes - does the browser ever do the latter?

interviewQuestions.question: Explain the purpose of the `<track>` element's `kind` attribute, why captions matter beyond accessibility compliance, and what browser autoplay policies have to do with video embedding.
interviewQuestions.answer:
**The `kind` attribute on `<track>`** distinguishes between several different purposes a text track can serve, all delivered as WebVTT files but interpreted differently by the player:

- `captions` - a transcription of dialogue *and* significant non-speech audio (sound effects, music cues, speaker identification), intended for users who are deaf or hard of hearing, or anyone watching without sound.
- `subtitles` - assumes the viewer can hear the audio but may not understand the spoken language; typically a straight translation of dialogue, without describing non-speech sounds.
- `chapters` - navigation markers that let a player offer a jump-to-section menu, without displaying any text overlay during normal playback.
- `descriptions` - a track describing important visual information for blind or low-vision users, generally surfaced via a separate audio-description channel or synthesized speech rather than as an on-screen caption overlay.

```html
<track src="captions-en.vtt" kind="captions" srclang="en" label="English" default>
```

**Why captions matter beyond compliance**: captions are essential for deaf and hard-of-hearing users, but their value extends much further in practice - a large share of video views on social platforms and in public/office settings happen with sound off or on mute by default, making captions the only way many viewers absorb the content at all. Caption text is also fully indexable by search engines (unlike the audio track itself), which can materially improve a video's discoverability, and supporting multiple `srclang` tracks extends a single video's reach to viewers who don't speak its original language without needing to produce a dubbed version.

**Autoplay policies**: every major browser restricts the `autoplay` attribute to prevent unsolicited sound, since unexpected audio has historically been one of the most disruptive and disliked web behaviors. The near-universal rule across browsers is that `autoplay` only reliably succeeds when the media is also `muted` (or, in some browsers, after the user has previously interacted with that site in a way the browser's heuristics consider meaningful engagement). Even then, individual browsers, mobile operating systems, and user-level "reduce data usage" or battery-saving settings can still override and block autoplay outright, so any design relying on it must have a sensible fallback (such as a visible play button) for when autoplay simply doesn't happen, rather than assuming it always will.

```html
<video autoplay muted loop playsinline>
  <source src="background-loop.mp4" type="video/mp4">
</video>
```

A reliably successful autoplay strategy therefore combines `muted` with a design that works equally well if autoplay is blocked and the video instead sits paused on its poster frame until a user explicitly presses play.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A marketing team wants a hero section with a muted, looping background video of product footage, and separately wants their tutorial videos to reach an international audience who don't speak the video's original recorded language.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Assuming autoplay will always succeed and designing a layout that looks broken if it's silently blocked by the browser; using subtitles when captions are actually needed (losing non-speech audio cues that matter for accessibility); forgetting the default attribute on track, leaving the viewer to manually enable captions through the player's menu every time.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
What specific conditions does a browser typically use to decide whether a site has earned enough prior user engagement to allow unmuted autoplay?
How would you provide an audio-description track for a video that contains important visual information never mentioned in the dialogue?

topics.title: Iframes
topics.summary: Embed external content with iframe and understand the security controls - sandbox and allow - that constrain what embedded content can do.

lessons.title: Embedding Content with iframe
lessons.contentMarkdown: An ` ``` - `src` - the URL of the document to embed. - `width` / `height` - the iframe's rendered size on the page (the content inside scales or scrolls to fit, depending on that document's own responsiveness). - `title` - **required for accessibility**; screen readers announce it to describe the embedded content's purpose, since an iframe otherwise has no inherent accessible name. Every iframe should have a concise, descriptive title. ## loading="lazy" Just like ``, iframes support deferred loading for embeds positioned below the initial viewport: ```html ``` This defers fetching the embedded page entirely until the user scrolls near it, which matters a lot for iframe-heavy pages (like ones embedding several YouTube videos or ads), since each iframe loads an entirely separate document with its own network requests and JavaScript execution. ## Same-Origin vs Cross-Origin Iframes An iframe can embed a page from the same website (same-origin) or a completely different website (cross-origin). The browser's **Same-Origin Policy** strictly restricts what JavaScript on the parent page can read from or do to a cross-origin iframe's content, and vice versa, as a fundamental security boundary - the parent page cannot, for example, read form values typed inside a cross-origin iframe, or arbitrarily manipulate its DOM. Communication between a page and a cross-origin iframe it embeds is only possible through the deliberately narrow `window.postMessage()` API, which both sides must explicitly opt into using. This isolation is exactly why iframes are considered reasonably safe for embedding third-party content (a payment form, an ad) without that content being able to freely read or tamper with the rest of your page - and it's also why embedding *your own* content across subdomains sometimes requires extra configuration to communicate as intended.

codeExamples.description: A lazily-loaded iframe embedding a third-party video, with a required accessible title
codeExamples.code:
<iframe
  src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/dQw4w9WgXcQ"
  width="560"
  height="315"
  title="Product demo: setting up your first project"
  loading="lazy">
</iframe>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a 560x315 embedded video player. The actual YouTube page content is not fetched by the browser until the user scrolls this iframe into (or near) the viewport. A screen reader announces the iframe's region as 'Product demo: setting up your first project' due to the title attribute.

lessons.title: Iframe Security: sandbox and allow
lessons.contentMarkdown:
Because an iframe can embed arbitrary content from anywhere on the web, HTML gives you fine-grained attributes to restrict exactly what that embedded content is permitted to do.

## The sandbox Attribute

Adding `sandbox` (with no value) to an iframe applies the maximum set of restrictions at once: it disables script execution, form submission, pop-ups, top-level navigation, treats the embedded content as coming from a unique, opaque origin (even if it's actually same-origin), and more.

```html
<iframe src="https://untrusted-widget.example.com" sandbox title="Third-party widget"></iframe>
```

You then selectively **re-enable** only the specific capabilities the embedded content actually needs, as a space-separated list of tokens:

```html
<iframe
  src="https://trusted-partner.example.com/checkout"
  sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms allow-same-origin"
  title="Checkout widget">
</iframe>
```

Common tokens include:
- `allow-scripts` - permits JavaScript execution inside the iframe.
- `allow-forms` - permits form submission.
- `allow-same-origin` - lets the embedded content be treated as its actual origin (rather than a forced unique opaque origin), which is required for it to access its own cookies/localStorage normally.
- `allow-popups` - permits the content to open new windows/tabs.
- `allow-top-navigation` - permits the embedded content to navigate the *entire* top-level page away from your site, which is rarely something you want to grant to untrusted content.

The security principle here is the **principle of least privilege**: start from zero capabilities (`sandbox` with no tokens) and add back only what is strictly necessary, rather than starting from an unrestricted iframe and trying to think of everything to disable.

## The allow Attribute (Permissions Policy)

`allow` is a separate mechanism controlling access to specific powerful browser features and APIs, such as camera, microphone, geolocation, and fullscreen.

```html
<iframe
  src="https://meet.example.com/room/123"
  allow="camera; microphone; fullscreen"
  title="Video conference room">
</iframe>
```

Without the corresponding token listed in `allow`, an embedded page is blocked from using that feature at all, even if it requests permission from the user - this gives the embedding page (not just the embedded site) a say over which sensitive device capabilities third-party content is allowed to even attempt to access.

## Why Both Matter Together

`sandbox` restricts general web-platform capabilities (scripts, forms, navigation, popups); `allow` specifically governs powerful device/feature APIs. A video-conferencing widget embedded via iframe, for example, typically needs `allow="camera; microphone"` granted explicitly, in addition to whatever `sandbox` tokens its underlying JavaScript functionality requires.

codeExamples.description: A tightly sandboxed iframe for an untrusted third-party ad, granting only the minimum required capabilities
codeExamples.code:
<iframe
  src="https://ad-network.example.com/banner/482"
  sandbox="allow-scripts"
  width="300"
  height="250"
  title="Advertisement">
</iframe>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a 300x250 ad banner. The embedded page can run its own JavaScript (allow-scripts), but cannot submit forms, cannot open popups, cannot navigate the parent page away from the current site, and is treated as coming from a unique, isolated origin with no access to the embedding site's cookies or storage.

codeExamples.description: An iframe granted camera and microphone access for a trusted video conferencing embed via the allow attribute
codeExamples.code:
<iframe
  src="https://meet.example.com/room/123"
  allow="camera; microphone; fullscreen"
  width="800"
  height="600"
  title="Video conference room">
</iframe>
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The embedded conferencing page is permitted to request camera, microphone, and fullscreen access from the user; without the matching tokens listed in allow, the browser would block those permission requests outright regardless of what the embedded page itself asks for.

interviewQuestions.question: What is an `<iframe>` used for, and why does it need a `title` attribute?
interviewQuestions.answer:
An `<iframe>` embeds an entirely separate HTML document inside a rectangular region of the current page. Each iframe has its own independent browsing context: its own DOM, its own JavaScript execution environment, and typically its own network requests, distinct from the parent page that embeds it.

Common real-world uses include embedding a map (like Google Maps), a video from a platform like YouTube, a payment or checkout widget from a third-party processor, a social media post embed, or a chat widget.

```html
<iframe
  src="https://www.example.com/map"
  width="600"
  height="450"
  title="Map of our downtown office location">
</iframe>
```

The `title` attribute provides an accessible name for the iframe's region. Without it, a screen reader user navigating the page has no description of what the embedded content actually is before entering it - they might hear only "iframe" with no further context, forcing them to explore its contents blindly just to find out. A short, descriptive title (e.g., "Map of our downtown office location" rather than just "Map") lets a screen reader user immediately understand what the embedded region contains and decide whether to explore it further.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A website embeds a customer support chat widget via iframe without a title attribute, and a screen reader user reports they can't tell what the embedded region on the page actually is before tabbing into it.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Omitting the title attribute entirely; writing a vague, unhelpful title like 'frame' or 'embed'; assuming iframe content automatically inherits accessibility context from the surrounding page, when it is actually a fully separate document.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
Does the title attribute on an iframe have any effect on SEO or search engine crawling of the embedded content?
How would you make an iframe's embedded content responsive to the width of its container?

interviewQuestions.question: What does the `sandbox` attribute do on an `<iframe>`, and how do you use its tokens to grant only the specific capabilities embedded content actually needs?
interviewQuestions.answer:
`sandbox` applies a set of security restrictions to an iframe's embedded content. Used with **no value at all**, it applies the maximum possible restriction: it disables JavaScript execution, blocks form submission, prevents opening popups, prevents the embedded content from navigating the top-level page, and forces the content to be treated as coming from a unique, isolated ("opaque") origin rather than its real one - even if the content is technically hosted on the same domain as the parent page.

```html
<iframe src="https://widget.example.com" sandbox title="Embedded widget"></iframe>
```

From that fully-locked-down baseline, you selectively re-enable only the specific capabilities the embedded content genuinely requires, by listing space-separated tokens as the attribute's value:

```html
<iframe
  src="https://widget.example.com"
  sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms"
  title="Embedded widget">
</iframe>
```

Commonly used tokens include `allow-scripts` (JavaScript execution), `allow-forms` (form submission), `allow-same-origin` (treats the content as its real origin, needed for it to access its own cookies/storage normally), `allow-popups` (opening new windows), and `allow-top-navigation` (navigating the entire parent tab away - rarely something you should grant to untrusted content).

The underlying approach is the principle of least privilege: start from zero permissions and add back only what is demonstrably needed, rather than starting unrestricted and trying to enumerate every risk to block. This matters most when embedding content you do not fully control or trust - third-party ads, user-submitted embeds, widgets from external vendors - since a compromised or malicious embedded page is then contained to only the narrow set of capabilities you explicitly granted it.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A content platform allows users to embed custom HTML widgets inside their profile pages via iframe, and the security team needs to ensure a malicious widget cannot steal the platform's own session cookies or redirect visitors to a phishing site.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Granting allow-same-origin together with allow-scripts without realizing that combination can let the embedded content access anything the real origin's cookies/storage would normally allow, effectively undoing much of the isolation sandbox was meant to provide if the iframe's src is actually same-origin with sensitive data; omitting sandbox entirely for 'convenience' during development and forgetting to add it back before shipping; assuming sandbox alone is sufficient without also considering Content-Security-Policy headers for defense in depth.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
Why can combining allow-scripts and allow-same-origin on a same-origin iframe be particularly risky compared to using them on a genuinely cross-origin iframe?
How does the sandbox attribute interact with an iframe that also has an allow attribute for camera/microphone access?

interviewQuestions.question: What is clickjacking, and how do response headers like `X-Frame-Options` and the CSP `frame-ancestors` directive relate to iframes and this attack?
interviewQuestions.answer:
**Clickjacking** is an attack where a malicious site embeds a victim site inside an `<iframe>`, then visually disguises or conceals it (commonly by setting the iframe's CSS `opacity` near zero and layering deceptive content on top), tricking a user into clicking on what appears to be an innocuous button, while the click is actually registered by the hidden, embedded victim page underneath. This can be used, for example, to trick a logged-in user into unknowingly clicking a "Delete Account" or "Authorize Payment" button on a legitimate site, believing they're interacting with the attacker's unrelated page.

The critical point: this attack relies entirely on the attacker's ability to embed the *victim* site inside their own page's iframe. The defense, therefore, is not something the iframe's own `sandbox` or `allow` attributes can provide (those attributes are set by the page doing the *embedding*, and an attacker obviously won't restrict their own malicious page). Instead, the victim site must tell browsers, via an HTTP response header, "do not allow me to be embedded in anyone else's iframe at all" (or only by specifically trusted origins).

Two mechanisms accomplish this:

1. **`X-Frame-Options`** - an older HTTP response header, sent by the server hosting the content that might be embedded. Common values: `DENY` (refuse to be framed by anyone, including the same site) or `SAMEORIGIN` (allow framing only by pages on the exact same origin).

```
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
```

2. **Content-Security-Policy's `frame-ancestors` directive** - the modern, more flexible replacement, also sent as a response header, which can specify an exact allow-list of origins permitted to embed the page.

```
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://trusted-partner.example.com
```

`frame-ancestors` supersedes `X-Frame-Options` wherever both are present and supported, and is generally preferred today since it allows a precise list of trusted embedding origins rather than just a same-origin-or-nothing binary choice.

It's worth being precise about where responsibility lies: these headers protect a site *from being maliciously embedded elsewhere*; the `sandbox`/`allow` attributes covered earlier protect a site *from content it chooses to embed*. A robust security posture needs both: send `frame-ancestors`/`X-Frame-Options` on pages containing sensitive actions so they cannot be clickjacked by other sites, and apply `sandbox` restrictions on any iframe your own pages embed, since you can't fully trust arbitrary third-party content either.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A banking web application discovers, during a penetration test, that its 'Transfer Funds' confirmation page can be embedded in an iframe on an external attacker-controlled site and visually hidden beneath a disguised game, allowing a clickjacking attack against logged-in users.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Confusing iframe-embedding attributes like sandbox (which govern content you embed) with response headers like frame-ancestors (which govern whether your own content can be embedded elsewhere) - these solve opposite-direction problems; relying only on JavaScript-based frame-busting scripts (e.g., checking window.top !== window.self) as the sole defense, which can be bypassed and is far less reliable than the proper HTTP header approach; setting X-Frame-Options but forgetting it is superseded by frame-ancestors where supported, leading to inconsistent protection across different header combinations.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How would you configure frame-ancestors to allow your own site to embed its own pages in an iframe (for an internal admin dashboard, say) while blocking every other origin?
Why are JavaScript-only frame-busting techniques considered an unreliable primary defense against clickjacking?

topics.title: Tables
topics.summary: Build tabular data layouts with thead, tbody, tr, td, and th, and make them accessible with scope and caption.

lessons.title: Building a Table with thead/tbody/tr/td/th
lessons.contentMarkdown:
HTML tables exist to present **genuinely tabular data** - information with real rows and columns, like a pricing comparison, a schedule, or a spreadsheet export. They should never be used purely to achieve a visual page layout; that job belongs to CSS Grid or Flexbox. ## The Core Elements ```html
Plan Price Storage
Basic $5/mo 10 GB
Pro $15/mo 100 GB
``` - `` - the outer wrapper for the entire table. - `` - groups the header row(s), typically containing column labels. - `` - groups the main body rows of data. Every table should have at least one `` (browsers insert one implicitly if omitted, but writing it explicitly is clearer). - `` - a table row, used inside both `` and `` (and ``). - `` groups a summary row, often totals, typically placed visually at the bottom of the table regardless of its position in the source markup. ```html ``` ## Why th vs td Matters, Not Just Visually Using `
` - a header cell, used for column or row labels. Browsers render it bold and centered by default. - `` - a standard data cell. ## tfoot A `
Total $20/mo 110 GB
` instead of `` for header cells is not just a styling shortcut - screen readers specifically announce `` content as a header when a user navigates into the corresponding data cells, helping them understand what each piece of data represents without needing to re-read the entire row or column every time. A table built entirely out of styled `` cells loses this structural information, even if it looks visually identical.

codeExamples.description: A pricing table using thead, tbody, tfoot, th, and td correctly
codeExamples.code:
Plan Price Storage
Basic $5/mo 10 GB
Pro $15/mo 100 GB
Total $20/mo 110 GB
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a three-column table: a bold header row reading 'Plan / Price / Storage', two data rows for Basic and Pro plans, and a summary row at the bottom reading 'Total / $20/mo / 110 GB'. A screen reader announces 'Plan, column header' etc. when navigating into cells, and reads the relevant column header alongside each data cell's value.

lessons.title: Spanning Cells and Table Accessibility
lessons.contentMarkdown:
Real-world tables are often more complex than a simple grid - cells sometimes need to span multiple columns or rows, and larger tables need extra markup to stay understandable for assistive technology. ## colspan and rowspan `colspan` makes a cell stretch across multiple columns; `rowspan` makes it stretch across multiple rows. ```html
Q1 2026
Revenue Expenses
$120,000 $85,000
``` Here, the "Q1 2026" header cell spans across both columns beneath it, acting as a merged title row. ```html
Engineering Alice
Bob
``` Here, "Engineering" spans vertically across two rows, since both Alice and Bob belong to that single department. ## The scope Attribute For tables with more than a very simple structure, add `scope` to each `` to explicitly declare whether it is a header for a column or a row, removing any ambiguity for assistive technology about which cells it labels. ```html
Name Role
Alice Engineer
``` `scope="col"` means "this header labels every cell in this column"; `scope="row"` means "this header labels every cell in this row." This becomes especially important once a table mixes column headers and row headers together, as in the example above. ## caption `` provides a title for the entire table, immediately as the table's first child, and is announced by screen readers before the table's contents, giving context before the user starts navigating individual cells. ```html ...
Team Directory - Engineering Department
Name Role
``` A `` is strongly preferable to a plain heading or paragraph placed just before the table, since it is programmatically tied to that specific table and announced as part of navigating into it, regardless of where in the DOM the user's focus came from.

codeExamples.description: An accessible staff directory table using caption, scope, and a rowspan for a shared department label
codeExamples.code:
Team Directory - Engineering Department
Department Name Role
Engineering Alice Chen Senior Engineer
Bob Martinez Engineer
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a captioned table titled 'Team Directory - Engineering Department' with three columns. 'Engineering' appears once, visually spanning both staff rows via rowspan. A screen reader announces the caption first, then correctly associates 'Engineering', 'Name', and 'Role' as headers for each corresponding data cell.

codeExamples.description: A merged header spanning two columns using colspan
codeExamples.code:
Q1 2026
Revenue Expenses
$120,000 $85,000
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Renders a top header cell reading 'Q1 2026' stretched visually across both columns, with 'Revenue' and 'Expenses' as narrower sub-headers beneath it, followed by one row of matching numeric data.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between `<th>` and `<td>`, and why does the distinction matter beyond visual styling?
interviewQuestions.answer:
`` defines a **header cell** - a label describing what a row or column of data represents. `` defines a standard **data cell** containing an actual value. ```html
Product Price
Widget $9.99
``` Visually, browsers render `` content bold and centered by default, while `` content is left-aligned and normal weight - but that visual difference is only a default stylesheet convenience, not the main point, and can be completely overridden with CSS either way. The real significance is **semantic and accessible**: screen readers specifically recognize `` elements as column or row headers. When a screen reader user navigates into a data cell, many screen readers will announce the relevant header text alongside that cell's value (for example, announcing "Price: $9.99" rather than just "$9.99"), helping the user understand what each number or value actually represents without needing to separately track which column or row they're in. A table built entirely from `` cells, even if visually styled to look identical to one using proper `` headers, loses this association entirely for non-visual users.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A finance dashboard renders a data table entirely with <td> elements, applying bold CSS styling to the first row purely to make it look like a header, and a screen reader user reports that the numbers read aloud have no indication of which column each one belongs to.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Using CSS to visually bold a td to fake a header row instead of using a real th element; assuming th is purely a styling shortcut with no semantic consequence; forgetting that th cells can also represent row headers, not just column headers.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How would the scope attribute refine the relationship between a th and the cells it labels in a more complex table?
What is the difference between how th is announced inside <thead> versus inside a row within <tbody>?

interviewQuestions.question: How do `colspan` and `rowspan` work, and what kind of table layout would require combining both on the same table?
interviewQuestions.answer:
`colspan` and `rowspan` are attributes placed on a `` or `` that make that single cell occupy more than one column or row, respectively, within the table's grid. - `colspan="2"` makes a cell stretch horizontally across two columns, meaning the following row(s) effectively have one fewer explicit cell needed to fill that width. - `rowspan="2"` makes a cell stretch vertically across two rows, meaning the following row needs one fewer explicit cell in that column position. ```html
Region 2026 Sales
Q1 Q2
West $42,000 $51,000
``` In this example, "Region" spans two rows vertically (since the "2026 Sales" super-header occupies a whole extra row above the Q1/Q2 sub-headers), while "2026 Sales" spans two columns horizontally (covering both the Q1 and Q2 columns beneath it). This combined pattern - a row header needing to span down past a multi-column grouped header above it - is exactly the kind of layout that commonly requires both attributes working together: a complex financial report, a class schedule with merged time slots, or a multi-level comparison table with grouped column categories. When building tables like this, it helps to sketch the final grid on paper first and count exactly how many ``/`` cells are actually needed in each ``, since spanning cells reduce how many additional cells that row needs - a common source of broken-looking tables is miscounting cells after adding a span.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A company builds a quarterly sales report table where each region's row header needs to align with two sub-columns (Q1 and Q2) grouped beneath one shared 'Sales' header spanning both of them, visually matching how the data is organized in the underlying spreadsheet.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Miscounting how many additional td/th cells a row needs after a previous row's cell spans down into it with rowspan; using colspan/rowspan purely to force a visual layout for unrelated content rather than to represent genuinely merged, related data; forgetting that scope needs to be reconsidered carefully on tables that use spanning headers, since a single scope="col" or scope="row" may no longer fully describe which cells a spanning header actually covers.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How does scope need to be adjusted on a th that also uses colspan to span multiple columns?
What happens visually if a row's cell count, accounting for spans carried over from previous rows, doesn't add up to match the table's actual column count?

interviewQuestions.question: Beyond `scope`, what is the `headers`/`id` attribute pairing used for in complex tables, and when does a table's structure become complex enough to need it instead of relying on `scope` alone?
interviewQuestions.answer:
For simple tables - a single row of column headers, or a single column of row headers, each header clearly and unambiguously labeling an entire row or column - the `scope="col"`/`scope="row"` attribute on each `` is sufficient for assistive technology to correctly associate headers with data cells. However, some tables have genuinely **multi-dimensional or irregular header structures** that `scope` cannot fully express - for example, a table with two levels of column headers (a grouped super-header spanning several sub-headers), where a given data cell is actually described by *multiple* headers at once (both its sub-column header and the group header above it, plus possibly a row header too). In these cases, HTML provides a more explicit, cell-by-cell association mechanism: the `id` attribute on each ``, paired with the `headers` attribute on each ``, which lists the exact `id`s of every header cell that applies to it, space-separated. ```html
Quarterly Revenue by Region
2026 Sales
Q1 Q2
West $42,000 $51,000
``` Here, the data cell "$42,000" explicitly declares that it is described by three different header cells at once: the row header "West," the column sub-header "Q1," and the grouping super-header "2026 Sales" - a relationship that a single `scope` value on one `` cannot capture, since `scope` only expresses a simple one-to-many "this header labels this whole row/column" relationship, not an arbitrary many-to-one mapping of exactly which headers apply to one specific cell. The practical guideline: reach for `scope` first, since it covers the vast majority of real-world tables with far less markup. Only escalate to the more verbose `id`/`headers` pairing when a table's structure is genuinely irregular or multi-level enough that `scope` cannot unambiguously describe which headers apply to which cells - trying to force `scope` onto a table that's structurally too complex for it typically produces header associations that are technically present but factually wrong or incomplete for at least some cells.
interviewQuestions.scenario: A financial reporting tool renders a table with two levels of column headers - a top-level 'Sales' header spanning both a Q1 and Q2 sub-column - combined with row headers identifying each region, and an accessibility audit flags that scope alone is producing ambiguous header announcements for some cells.
interviewQuestions.commonMistakes: Reaching for the far more verbose id/headers pattern on every table by default, even simple ones where scope alone would suffice; building the id/headers relationships but introducing typos in the headers attribute's space-separated id list, silently breaking the association for that cell; forgetting that id values must be unique across the entire page, not just within the table, which can cause conflicts when multiple similarly-structured tables appear on one page.
interviewQuestions.followUps:
How would a screen reader's announcement differ for a cell associated via headers="west q1 sales-group" compared to one relying only on scope?
At what point would restructuring the table's actual data (e.g., flattening a multi-level header into separate simpler tables) be a better solution than adding complex headers/id markup?

topics.title: Ordered, Unordered, and Description Lists
topics.summary: Choose the right list type for your content: ul for unordered items, ol for sequential items, and dl for term/definition pairs.

lessons.title: Ordered and Unordered Lists
lessons.contentMarkdown:
Lists are one of the most common ways to structure content on the web, from navigation menus to step-by-step instructions. ## Unordered Lists `
    ` represents a list of items where **order does not carry meaning** - the items could be rearranged without changing the content's meaning. Each item is wrapped in an `
  • ` (list item). ```html
    • Milk
    • Eggs
    • Bread
    ``` By default, browsers render each `
  • ` with a bullet point marker, though this is purely a CSS default (`list-style-type`) and can be changed or removed entirely. ## Ordered Lists `
      ` represents a list where **sequence matters** - numbered steps in a recipe, ranked results, or a table of contents. ```html
      1. Preheat the oven to 350°F.
      2. Mix the dry ingredients.
      3. Fold in the wet ingredients.
      ``` ## Useful Attributes on ol ```html
      1. Step five
      2. Step six
      1. Third place
      2. Second place
      3. First place
      1. Option A
      2. Option B
      ``` - `start` sets the numeric value of the first item (useful when continuing a list that was split across separate `
        ` blocks). - `reversed` counts downward instead of upward. - `type` changes the marker style: `1` (default, numbers), `A`/`a` (uppercase/lowercase letters), `I`/`i` (uppercase/lowercase Roman numerals). ## Choosing ul vs ol Ask: "if I shuffled these items randomly, would the meaning change?" If yes (a recipe's steps, a ranking), use `
          `. If no (a shopping list, a set of feature bullet points), use `
            `. This choice should be based on the content's actual meaning, not on which marker style looks better - that's a job for CSS.

lessons.title: Description Lists with dl, dt, and dd
lessons.contentMarkdown:
Beyond ordered and unordered lists, HTML provides a third list type specifically for **name/value** or **term/description** pairs: the description list.

## Structure

```html
<dl>
  <dt>HTML</dt>
  <dd>HyperText Markup Language, used to structure content on the web.</dd>

  <dt>CSS</dt>
  <dd>Cascading Style Sheets, used to style and lay out HTML content.</dd>
</dl>
```

- `<dl>` - wraps the entire description list.
- `<dt>` - the term (or name) being described.
- `<dd>` - the description (or value) associated with the preceding term.

## Multiple Terms or Multiple Descriptions

A single term can have multiple descriptions, and multiple terms can share one description, by simply listing consecutive `<dt>`/`<dd>` elements without anything else between them.

```html
<dl>
  <dt>Monday</dt>
  <dt>Wednesday</dt>
  <dt>Friday</dt>
  <dd>Gym open 6am-9pm</dd>

  <dt>Saturday</dt>
  <dd>Gym open 8am-6pm</dd>
  <dd>Pool open 10am-4pm</dd>
</dl>
```

Here, three separate days all share the same single description, and Saturday itself has two separate descriptions.

## Common Real-World Uses

Beyond glossaries and dictionary-style definitions, `<dl>` is a semantically appropriate choice for:
- Metadata display (author: ..., published: ..., category: ...)
- FAQ sections (question as `<dt>`, answer as `<dd>`)
- Key-value configuration summaries
- Any content genuinely structured as a list of "label, then its associated value(s)"

```html
<dl>
  <dt>Author</dt>
  <dd>Priya Shah</dd>
  <dt>Published</dt>
  <dd>March 3, 2026</dd>
</dl>
```

Using `<dl>` for this kind of content is more meaningful to assistive technology and more semantically honest than simulating the same visual layout with a generic `<div>`/`<span>` combination or a misused table.
